Final predictions after 200 steps: [1.00, −0.99, −1.00, 1.00] versus targets [1, −1, −1, 1] — the network has memorized all four points (computed, seed 42). The arresting feature is iteration 1: the loss jumps from 2.23 to 7.85 before collapsing. That overshoot is the learning-rate-1.0 step kicking the weights past the minimum on the first move; on a 4-point toy it recovers immediately, but on real data a step that large would diverge — a concrete reminder of why η is normally ≪ 1 (see Diagnostics, §6). Because the notebook sets no seed, the exact loss trajectory differs run to run, though the qualitative story (early spike, then near-zero) is stable.

title: Neural Network Basics
Neural Network Basics
text:
6. Diagnostics & interpretation
What to watch when training an MLP:

The loss curve. Plot loss against iteration. It should fall and flatten. A loss that spikes or diverges (as at iteration 1 in §4, or worse) signals the learning rate η is too large; one that barely moves signals η too small or vanishing gradients. A train loss near zero while held-out loss climbs is overfitting (high variance); both losses stuck high is underfitting (too few hidden units / too little capacity).
Over- vs under-fitting via width and depth. The number of hidden units K and the number of layers are the network’s capacity dial. Too small ⇒ underfit; too large ⇒ overfit. The toy in §4 reaching zero training loss on 4 points with 28 parameters is overfitting by construction — it has far more parameters than data.
Vanishing gradients. With sigmoid or tanh, saturated units have g'(z) ≈ 0 (see §5), so the backprop signal −(y−f)·β_k·g'(z_k)·x_j is multiplied by ≈0 and upstream weights stop learning. This is the practical reason ReLU is the modern default activation, and why initialization scale matters.
Regularization. Two course tools fight overfitting: L2 weight decay (penalize large weights) and dropout (randomly zero a fraction of units during training, typically 0.2–0.5, train-only) — both detailed in §8 Mode B.


The capacity dial, and when a net is the wrong tool. A neural network’s bias–variance trade-off is governed by its width (K) and depth — more units/layers lower bias but raise variance, the same dial as polynomial degree in bias–variance. But the dial only pays off with enough data to constrain all those parameters. On small tabular problems that condition fails, and a random forest or gradient-boosted trees — which get strong nonlinear fits with little tuning and far less data — will usually win (Lecture 10, slide 15/15). The network’s flexibility is an asset only when data volume can cash it in.

title: Neural Network Basics
text:
7. Past-exam lens

How neural-network basics show up. They did not appear on the Spring-2025 exam (phase0/disagreements.md, R8 — not examined). The graded deep-learning content in the course centers on the PyTorch workflow and the regularization tools (L2, dropout) covered in Build a NN, not on the from-scratch autodiff MLP, which is a conceptual scaffold: it exists so that the forward pass, the backprop chain rule (§8), and the meaning of “a layer is a matrix multiply followed by an activation” are not a black box before you reach for a framework. If neural nets were examined, expect conceptual questions — architecture, the forward-pass formula, why nonlinearity matters, the role of η — rather than a from-scratch derivation under time pressure.

title: Neural Network Basics
text:
8. Math


Math is off. Use the Math toggle in the top bar to show the course-level derivation (and “full” for the rigorous version).


Mode A — course level. The course states the single-hidden-layer model and runs the forward pass as matrix multiplications (Lecture 9, slides 4–8/17; notebook 17_Neural_nets_basics.ipynb). With K hidden units, activation g(·), and p inputs X = (X_1,…,X_p), the model is f(X) = \beta_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \beta_k\, g\!\Bigl(w_{k0} + \sum_{j=1}^{p} w_{kj} X_j\Bigr) \qquad \text{(Lecture 9, slide 4/17).} This matches ISL Eq. 10.1 — slide 9/17 explicitly cites ISL (James, Witten, Hastie, Tibshirani, 2021). The course builds it in two steps (slide 6/17): (1) each hidden unit forms a pre-activation z_k = w_{k0} + \sum_j w_{kj} X_j and an activation A_k = g(z_k); (2) the output is a linear function of those activations, f(X) = \beta_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \beta_k A_k. Here K is the hidden-unit count, g(·) the activation, β_k the output-layer weights, w_{kj} the input→hidden weights, and w_{k0}/β_0 the biases (phase0/notation_table.md).
Stacked over an n\times p input matrix X, the forward pass is two matrix multiplies, each followed by an element-wise activation (slide 7/17): A = g\bigl(\mathbf{1}_n w_0^\top + X W^\top\bigr) \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times K}, \qquad Y = \beta_0 \mathbf{1}_n + A\beta \in \mathbb{R}^{n}, where W is the K\times p hidden-weight matrix, w_0 the K-vector of hidden biases, \beta = (\beta_1,\dots,\beta_K)^\top, and \mathbf{1}_n a length-n ones vector. “Each layer is a matrix multiply followed by an activation” is exactly what makes nets fast on GPUs (slide 7/17). The course activations (slide 8/17) are sigmoid g(z)=1/(1+e^{-z}) (same nonlinearity as logistic regression), ReLU g(z)=\max(0,z), and softmax g(z_i)=e^{z_i}/\sum_j e^{z_j} for multi-class output. The from-scratch notebook uses tanh for every neuron, including the output, so its targets lie in \{-1,+1\} (§3–§4). Foundations: gradient descent and the backprop appendix.


Mode B — full rigor. (Anchored to ESL §11.3–11.5, eqs 11.5–11.16; ISL §10.7, eqs 10.23–10.31.) In ESL’s notation the network has hidden-layer weights \alpha_{m\ell} (ESL’s \alpha = the course’s w_{kj}) and output weights \beta_{km}, with derived features Z_m = \sigma(\alpha_{0m}+\alpha_m^\top X), outputs T_k = \beta_{0k}+\beta_k^\top Z, and f_k(X)=g_k(T) (ESL 11.5), g_k the softmax for classification (ESL 11.6). The complete parameter set is \theta = \{\alpha_{0m},\alpha_m\}\cup\{\beta_{0k},\beta_k\} (ESL 11.8).
Fitting. For a quantitative response, fit by minimizing sum-of-squared errors R(\theta) = \sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\bigl(y_{ik}-f_k(x_i)\bigr)^2 \qquad \text{(ESL 11.9)}, (for classification, the cross-entropy/deviance R(\theta)=-\sum_i\sum_k y_{ik}\log f_k(x_i), ESL 11.10). The generic minimizer is gradient descent, called back-propagation here; the foundation — the step \theta^{(r+1)}=\theta^{(r)}-\eta\,\nabla R, conditions on the rate \eta, and convexity geometry — is in the gradient-descent appendix.
The back-propagation equations. Writing z_{mi}=\sigma(\alpha_{0m}+\alpha_m^\top x_i) and R(\theta)=\sum_i R_i (ESL 11.11), differentiation gives \frac{\partial R_i}{\partial \beta_{km}} = -2\bigl(y_{ik}-f_k(x_i)\bigr)\,g_k'(\beta_k^\top z_i)\,z_{mi}, \qquad
\frac{\partial R_i}{\partial \alpha_{m\ell}} = -\sum_{k=1}^{K} 2\bigl(y_{ik}-f_k(x_i)\bigr)\,g_k'(\beta_k^\top z_i)\,\beta_{km}\,\sigma'(\alpha_m^\top x_i)\,x_{i\ell} \quad \text{(ESL 11.12)}, and the gradient-descent update at iteration r+1 is \beta_{km}^{(r+1)}=\beta_{km}^{(r)}-\gamma_r\sum_i \partial R_i/\partial\beta_{km}^{(r)}, likewise for \alpha_{m\ell} (ESL 11.13), with \gamma_r the learning rate. Writing these as \partial R_i/\partial\beta_{km}=\delta_{ki}z_{mi} and \partial R_i/\partial\alpha_{m\ell}=s_{mi}x_{i\ell} (ESL 11.14) defines the error signals \delta_{ki} (output) and s_{mi} (hidden); they satisfy the back-propagation equation s_{mi} = \sigma'(\alpha_m^\top x_i)\sum_{k=1}^{K}\beta_{km}\,\delta_{ki} \qquad \text{(ESL 11.15)}, implemented as a two-pass algorithm: a forward pass fixes the weights and computes \hat f_k(x_i); a backward pass computes the output errors \delta_{ki} and back-propagates them via (11.15) to the hidden errors s_{mi} (ESL §11.4). This is the δ-recursion the course’s slide-14 chain rule specializes to: with one output and identity output activation, \delta_{ki}\equiv -(y_i-f_i) and s_{mi}\equiv -(y_i-f_i)\beta_k\,g'(z_k), recovering the course gradients \partial L_i/\partial\beta_k=-(y_i-f_i)A_{ik} and \partial L_i/\partial w_{kj}=-(y_i-f_i)\beta_k g'(z_k)x_j — note the course reserves \delta for the update step, not the error signal (phase0/disagreements.md [R9-10]). ISL gives the same two gradients as eqs 10.29–10.30. Full derivation: backprop appendix.
Weight decay (L2). ESL §11.5 adds a penalty R(\theta)+\lambda J(\theta) with J(\theta) = \sum_{km}\beta_{km}^2 + \sum_{m\ell}\alpha_{m\ell}^2 \qquad \text{(ESL 11.16)}, which penalizes all weights (its only effect on training is to add 2\beta_{km} and 2\alpha_{m\ell} to the respective gradients), and recommends standardizing inputs and random starting weights over [-0.7,+0.7]. ESL also offers the weight-elimination penalty \sum\beta_{km}^2/(1+\beta_{km}^2)+\sum\alpha_{m\ell}^2/(1+\alpha_{m\ell}^2) (ESL 11.17), which shrinks small weights harder.






Note



[VERIFY] resolved — L2 penalty scope ([R9-9]). The three sources genuinely diverge on which weights L2 penalizes. Lecture 9 slide 16/17 writes L_\text{reg}=\tfrac12\sum_i(y_i-f)^2+\lambda\sum_{k,j}w_{kj}^2 — summing only over the hidden weights w_{kj}, not the output weights \beta_k. ESL §11.5 eq 11.16 penalizes all weights (\alpha and \beta). ISL §10.7.2 eq 10.31 sits in between and confirms the slide’s instinct: in its MNIST example “W_1 and W_2 were penalized, while the relatively few weights B of the output layer were not penalized at all.” Meanwhile notebook 19 (Build a NN) implements lambda_reg * sum(p.pow(2)) over all parameters — i.e. it matches ESL, not the slide it accompanies. Resolution per GR4: the slide form is primary for the course (hidden weights only); ESL’s all-weights form is the formal anchor; the slide-vs-ESL gap is real and the notebook silently follows ESL. Not silently reconciled — both forms shown (read directly: Lecture 9 slide 16; ESL p420 eq 11.16; ISL p430 eq 10.31).


Dropout & SGD. ESL frames online updates (one observation at a time, a training epoch = one sweep) as a special case of (11.13) with single-summand sums (ESL §11.4); the course adds dropout — randomly zeroing units during training (rate 0.2–0.5, train-only), interpretable as an ensemble over sub-networks (Lecture 9, slide 17/17).

title: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
text: Linear family · the supervised cousin of PCA: one model that does both classification and dimensionality reduction by projecting onto the directions that pull the classes apart. Siblings: Logistic Regression (also a linear classifier, but no dimensionality reduction and fewer distributional assumptions), QDA (one covariance per class), PCA (unsupervised — variance, not class separation), kNN (non-parametric alternative).

title: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
text:
1. Essence
Linear Discriminant Analysis takes labelled data and finds the direction(s) along which the classes are most cleanly separated, then either reports a class for each point (classifier) or hands back the low-dimensional projection (dimensionality reduction). The guiding idea is a single trade-off, the Fisher criterion: choose the projection that makes the class means sit far apart (large between-class variance) while each class stays tight around its own mean (small within-class variance) (Lecture 3, slide 8/20; notebook 04_Linear_discriminant_analysis.ipynb, cell 2). Because that projection is a linear combination of the features, the resulting decision boundary is a straight line (or hyperplane), and a C-class problem yields at most C-1 useful discriminant directions — which is why two classes collapse to a single axis.
It is a parametric, generative model: it assumes each class is drawn from a Gaussian and — crucially — that all classes share one covariance matrix (Lecture 3, slide 10/20). Under those assumptions LDA is the Bayes-optimal linear classifier; it trains in essentially one pass (estimate the class means, the pooled covariance, and the priors), needs little data, and gives an interpretable boundary. The shared-covariance assumption is exactly what makes the boundary linear — relax it (one covariance per class) and you get the quadratic boundary of QDA instead.
LDA wears two hats at once, which is its distinctive feature. As a classifier it competes with logistic regression: both are linear, but LDA commits to the Gaussian/shared-covariance story while logistic regression models the log-odds directly and makes fewer distributional assumptions (Lecture 3, slide 11/20). As a dimensionality reducer it competes with PCA: PCA keeps the directions of greatest total variance ignoring labels, whereas LDA — being supervised — keeps the directions of greatest class separation (Lecture 3, slide 7/20).

title: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
section: 2. When to use / when not to use
text:
2. When to use / when not to use

Reach for LDA when…

The target is a class and you have two or more reasonably well-separated classes whose spreads (covariances) look similar (Lecture 3, slide 7/20).
You want an interpretable linear boundary and/or a supervised low-dimensional view of the data — LDA gives you both from one fit. On Iris it compresses 4 features to 2 discriminants that visibly separate the three species (see §4).
You want a fast, low-variance baseline classifier that needs little data — the model is just class means, a pooled covariance, and priors.
You plan to feed a downstream classifier a cheaper representation: LDA is “frequently used as a preprocessing step before applying classifiers like logistic regression” (notebook 04_…, cell 4).



Reach for something else when…

The classes have clearly different covariances (different shapes/orientations) → the shared-covariance assumption is wrong and the linear boundary underfits. Use QDA, which estimates a separate covariance per class and gives a quadratic boundary (Lecture 3, slide 10/20).
You want minimal distributional assumptions for a linear classifier → Logistic Regression models the log-odds directly without assuming Gaussian features; it is often the safer default when normality is doubtful (Lecture 3, slide 11/20).
You want dimensionality reduction but have no labels (or care about variance, not separation) → PCA is the unsupervised counterpart; LDA cannot run without y (it is supervised — “it requires the class labels to be passed … in the fit method”, notebook 04_…, cell 14).
The boundary is clearly non-linear → kNN or Decision Trees / Random Forests drop the linear-form assumption (more flexible, less interpretable, hungrier for data).

title: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
text:
3. Code idiom
The canonical course idiom is scikit-learn’s LinearDiscriminantAnalysis; the course also builds LDA from scratch via the eigendecomposition of S_W^{-1}S_B so the Fisher criterion is not a black box.
Canonical (sklearn) — (notebook 04_Linear_discriminant_analysis.ipynb, cell 8)
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis

# n_components: number of discriminant axes to keep after transform; must be ≤ #classes − 1
lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=1)   # 2-class toy data → at most 1 discriminant
lda.fit(X_train, y_train)                          # supervised: labels are REQUIRED
X_transformed = lda.transform(X_train)             # project onto the discriminant axis (dim reduction)
lda.predict(X_test)                                # class labels (classification)
lda.score(X_test, y_test)                          # mean accuracy
For multi-class dimensionality reduction the only change is n_components (notebook 04_…, cell 15) — and fit_transform does fit-then-project in one call:
lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=2)   # 3-class Iris → up to 2 discriminants (LD1, LD2)
X_train_lda = lda.fit_transform(X_train2, y_train2)  # fit on train, return its projection
X_test_lda  = lda.transform(X_test2)                 # project test with the SAME learned axes
The hyperparameters worth knowing (Lecture 3, slide 11/20): solver ∈ {svd (default, no covariance inversion, good for many features), lsqr, eigen}; shrinkage (regularizes the covariance estimate, only with lsqr/eigen); and n_components (the projection dimension, capped at #classes − 1). In notebook 04_… everything except n_components is left at its default. Useful attributes: coef_, means_, explained_variance_ratio_. Tip stressed in lecture: scale/standardize features first (Lecture 3, slide 11/20; Lecture 4, slide 4/11).
From scratch — eigendecomposition of S_W^{-1}S_B (notebook 04_…, cell 18; this is the Tier-1 variation that fills the gap cell 4 leaves: “we will not dive into all the mathematical details”). The heart of the class is: build the within- and between-class scatter, then take the eigenvectors of \Sigma^{-1}S_B:
# within-class scatter S_W (sum of per-class outer products), then pooled covariance
S_W = np.zeros((n_features, n_features))
for c in self.classes_:
    X_c = X[y == c]; mean_c = self.means_[c].reshape(-1, 1)
    for x in X_c:
        x = x.reshape(-1, 1)
        S_W += (x - mean_c) @ (x - mean_c).T
self.cov_ = S_W / (n_samples - len(self.classes_))   # unbiased pooled cov, "consistent with sklearn"

# between-class scatter S_B = Σ_c N_c (μ_c − μ)(μ_c − μ)ᵀ
S_B = np.zeros((n_features, n_features))
for c in self.classes_:
    mean_diff = self.means_[c].reshape(-1, 1) - self.overall_mean_
    S_B += self.class_count_[c] * (mean_diff @ mean_diff.T)

# generalized eigenproblem: discriminant axes = top eigenvectors of inv(Σ) @ S_B
A = np.linalg.inv(self.cov_) @ S_B
eigvals, eigvecs = np.linalg.eig(A)
idx = np.argsort(np.real(eigvals))[::-1]      # sort eigenvalues descending
self.W_ = np.real(eigvecs)[:, idx][:, :self.n_components]   # keep top n_components

Idiom variation worth knowing. The from-scratch predict does not project-then-threshold; it applies the Gaussian/Bayes discriminant rule directly, \delta_c(x) = x^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_c - \tfrac12\mu_c^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_c + \log\pi_c, and takes the argmax over classes (notebook 04_…, cell 18). This is the same maximum-a-posteriori rule sklearn uses, which is why the two implementations agree to the digit on the toy set (see §4). If you ever quote the from-scratch test accuracy, recompute it — the notebook does not store that number (phase0/disagreements.md [NB-10]); the value below was computed in the venv.

title: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
text:
4. Worked examples

Example 1 — toy 2-class set: classifier accuracy, sklearn vs from-scratch
The course generates a 2-feature, 2-class toy set and fits LDA as a classifier (notebook 04_…, cell 6):
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=200, n_features=2, n_redundant=0, n_informative=2,
                           n_clusters_per_class=1, class_sep=0.75, random_state=42)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.33, random_state=42)
LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=1).fit(X_train, y_train).score(X_test, y_test)
The stored notebook output is a test accuracy of 0.7424 (notebook 04_…, cell 13, stored output 0.7424242424242424). The modest score is the point, not a bug: class_sep=0.75 makes the two Gaussians overlap substantially, so even the Bayes-optimal linear boundary cannot do much better — a vivid reminder that accuracy is bounded by how separable the classes actually are, not by the model’s effort.
The from-scratch LDAFromScratch(n_components=1) (cell 18–19), fit on the same split, reaches the identical test accuracy of 0.7424 (train accuracy 0.7910 for both) — computed in the venv (./.venv/Scripts/python.exe, random_state=42), resolving the [VERIFY] flag in phase0/disagreements.md [NB-10]. The agreement is by design: both use the pooled (unbiased) covariance S_W/(n-C) and the same Bayes discriminant rule, so they are the same classifier, just coded twice. The single non-trivial eigenvalue of \Sigma^{-1}S_B is ≈ 77.4 (the second is numerically zero — there is only C-1 = 1 discriminant for two classes), computed in the venv.

This is the natural place to line LDA up against logistic regression: on a 2-class problem both draw a straight boundary, but LDA assumes the two clouds are Gaussian with a shared covariance whereas logistic regression just fits the log-odds. When that assumption roughly holds (as here, by construction), they land in the same neighbourhood; when it fails badly, logistic regression usually degrades more gracefully. See the 2D classification showdown.



Example 2 — Iris: LDA as supervised dimensionality reduction
On Iris (150 samples, 4 features, 3 species) LDA wears its other hat — squashing 4 features to 2 discriminants for visualization (notebook 04_…, cell 15):
iris = load_iris(); X2, y2 = iris.data, iris.target
X_train2, X_test2, y_train2, y_test2 = train_test_split(X2, y2, test_size=0.2, random_state=10)
lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=2)     # 3 classes → up to 2 discriminants
X_train_lda = lda.fit_transform(X_train2, y_train2)  # LD1, LD2 for the training set
X_test_lda  = lda.transform(X_test2)
The first discriminant carries almost everything: explained_variance_ratio_ ≈ [0.992, 0.008] — LD1 alone accounts for ~99.2 % of the between-class separation (computed in the venv, random_state=10). In the LD1–LD2 scatter the three species fall into cleanly separated bands, with setosa far from the other two. As a classifier on this split the same model scores 0.975 train / 1.00 test accuracy (computed in the venv) — but with only 30 test points the perfect test score is small-sample luck, not a claim that Iris is trivially separable; report it as “high” rather than overreading the exact 1.00.

Contrast with PCA on the same Iris data: PCA would pick the 2 directions of largest total variance ignoring the species labels, which need not be the directions that separate species. LDA’s 99.2 %-on-LD1 result is precisely what supervision buys you — it spends its budget on class separation, not raw spread. This is the canonical “supervised vs unsupervised dimensionality reduction” comparison.

title: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
text:
6. Diagnostics & interpretation
What to report and look at to decide whether an LDA model is working:

Accuracy / confusion matrix — LDA is a classifier first; report test accuracy (toy: 0.74) and, for multi-class, the confusion matrix to see which classes get confused (Lecture 4, slide 4/11 explicitly recommends confusion matrices).
explained_variance_ratio_ — for the dimensionality-reduction hat, this tells you how much class separation each discriminant captures (Iris: LD1 ≈ 99.2 %). A first discriminant near 1.0 means a 1D view loses almost nothing.
Check the shared-covariance assumption — if the classes visibly have different shapes/orientations, the linear boundary is mis-specified; that is the cue to move to QDA. Mild non-normality is usually tolerable (“robust to mild normality violations”, Lecture 4, slide 4/11).
Did you standardize? — scaling is stressed twice in lecture (L3 slide 11, L4 slide 4); on raw features with very different units the pooled covariance can be dominated by one feature.


Comparative diagnostic vs siblings: LDA gives you a generative story (class means + a shared covariance + priors), so you can read off how it would generate each class — where logistic regression gives only a discriminative boundary (the log-odds), and PCA gives variance-ranked axes with no notion of class at all. Choose the model whose output answers your question: “which class, and why” (LDA), “what are the odds” (logistic), or “what varies most” (PCA).

title: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
text:
7. Past-exam lens

How LDA shows up. LDA was not examined in the Spring-2025 take-home (phase0/concept_inventory.md; per rule R8 this absence is stated explicitly rather than glossed over) — the four assignments covered regression with regularization (Hitters), unsupervised PCA/K-means (WholesaleCustomers), trees/ensembles (WDBC), and a classifier comparison. LDA’s most natural exam framing, inferred from how Lecture 3 teaches it, is comparative: (i) as a 2-class linear classifier set against logistic regression — fit both, compare accuracy/boundaries, and discuss which assumptions each makes (LDA’s Gaussian/shared-covariance vs logistic’s distribution-free log-odds, Lecture 3 slide 11/20 gives the explicit comparison table); or (ii) as supervised dimensionality reduction set against PCA — show that LDA’s axes maximize class separation (Iris LD1 ≈ 99 %) while PCA’s maximize total variance. If LDA appears, the marks would rest on justifying the assumptions and the choice, exactly as the regularization task rewards justifying shrinkage.

title: Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA)
text:
8. Math


Math is off. Use the Math toggle in the top bar to show the course-level derivation (and “full” for the rigorous version).


Mode A — course level. The course frames LDA through Fisher’s criterion: find the projection direction w that pushes the class means apart while keeping each class tight (notebook 04_Linear_discriminant_analysis.ipynb, cell 2; Lecture 3, slide 8/20). Write the between-class and within-class scatter matrices S_B = \sum_{i=1}^{C} N_i\,(m_i-m)(m_i-m)^\top, \qquad S_W = \sum_{i=1}^{C}\sum_{x\in C_i}(x-m_i)(x-m_i)^\top, where m_i = \tfrac{1}{N_i}\sum_{x\in C_i} x is the mean of class i (size N_i) and m is the overall mean (slide 9/20). Fisher’s criterion is the ratio of projected between- to within-class variance, which we maximize: w = \arg\max_w \frac{w^\top S_B\, w}{w^\top S_W\, w}. Reading it: the numerator w^\top S_B w is how far apart the class means look after projecting onto w; the denominator w^\top S_W w is how spread out each class looks along w — so the ratio rewards separation and penalizes overlap. Setting the gradient of this ratio to zero turns it into a generalized eigenproblem whose top eigenvectors are the discriminant axes: S_W^{-1}S_B\, w = \lambda w \qquad \text{(cell 3; slide 9/20).} For two classes this collapses to a single closed form (only C-1=1 axis exists), and because S_B then has rank one the direction is simply w \propto S_W^{-1}(m_1-m_2) \qquad \text{(Lecture 3, slide 9/20)} — the line joining the two means, “rotated” by S_W^{-1} to undo the within-class spread. Local notation note (per phase0/notation_table.md): here \lambda denotes an LDA eigenvalue (not a regularization strength), m_i the class mean, N_i the class size, and w the discriminant direction (not a generic weight vector). See the linear-algebra appendix.


Mode B — full rigor. (Anchored to ESL §4.3, eqs 4.7–4.12 and 4.15–4.16; verified at PDF pp. 126–135 = printed pp. 106–116.) ESL derives LDA from decision theory, not from Fisher’s ratio. Let f_k(x) be the class-conditional density and \pi_k the prior of class k (with \sum_k\pi_k=1). Bayes’ theorem gives the posterior \Pr(G=k\mid X=x) = \frac{f_k(x)\,\pi_k}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K f_\ell(x)\,\pi_\ell} \qquad \text{(ESL 4.7),} so classifying to the largest posterior is Bayes-optimal. Now model each class as a multivariate Gaussian f_k(x) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{p/2}\lvert\Sigma_k\rvert^{1/2}}\,\exp\!\Bigl(-\tfrac12 (x-\mu_k)^\top\Sigma_k^{-1}(x-\mu_k)\Bigr) \qquad \text{(ESL 4.8).} LDA is the special case of a shared covariance \Sigma_k=\Sigma\ \forall k. Comparing two classes by their log-posterior ratio, \log\frac{\Pr(G=k\mid x)}{\Pr(G=\ell\mid x)} = \log\frac{\pi_k}{\pi_\ell} - \tfrac12(\mu_k+\mu_\ell)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell) + x^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mu_k-\mu_\ell) \qquad \text{(ESL 4.9),} which is linear in x: the shared \Sigma makes the normalizing constants and the quadratic term x^\top\Sigma^{-1}x cancel between the two classes. The boundary \{x:\Pr(G=k\mid x)=\Pr(G=\ell\mid x)\} is therefore a hyperplane. Equivalently, classify by G(x)=\arg\max_k \delta_k(x) using the linear discriminant functions \delta_k(x) = x^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k - \tfrac12\mu_k^\top\Sigma^{-1}\mu_k + \log\pi_k \qquad \text{(ESL 4.10)} — exactly the rule the from-scratch predict implements (notebook 04_…, cell 18), with the plug-in estimates \hat\pi_k=N_k/N, \hat\mu_k=\sum_{g_i=k}x_i/N_k, and the pooled covariance \hat\Sigma=\sum_{k}\sum_{g_i=k}(x_i-\hat\mu_k)(x_i-\hat\mu_k)^\top/(N-K) (the N-K denominator is why the notebook’s S_W/(n−C) “matches sklearn”). Why this matters: QDA. If the \Sigma_k are not assumed equal, the quadratic term survives and you get the quadratic discriminant \delta_k(x)=-\tfrac12\log\lvert\Sigma_k\rvert-\tfrac12(x-\mu_k)^\top\Sigma_k^{-1}(x-\mu_k)+\log\pi_k (ESL 4.12) — a curved boundary. Shared covariance ⇔ linear; per-class covariance ⇔ quadratic.
Equivalence to Fisher’s criterion. ESL §4.3.3 shows the Mode-A view is the same model. Writing B for the between-class covariance of the centroids and W for the within-class (pooled) covariance, Fisher’s “maximize between- over within-class variance” is the Rayleigh quotient \max_a \frac{a^\top B\, a}{a^\top W\, a} \qquad \text{(ESL 4.15)} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \max_a a^\top B\, a \ \text{ s.t. } a^\top W a = 1 \qquad \text{(ESL 4.16),} “a generalized eigenvalue problem, with a given by the largest eigenvalue of W^{-1}B” — identical in form to Mode A’s S_W^{-1}S_B w=\lambda w (B,W are ESL’s names for S_B,S_W, and B+W=T, the total covariance). ESL notes Fisher “arrived at this decomposition via a different route, without referring to Gaussian distributions at all,” yet it lands on the same discriminant directions — the two derivations agree (phase0/disagreements.md: LDA Fisher criterion and w\propto S_W^{-1}(m_1-m_2) match ESL §4.3; no flags). One subtlety ESL flags: the least-squares/Fisher route fixes the direction but the Gaussian route is needed to set the intercept (cut-point) — for two classes the two agree only when N_1=N_2 (ESL eq. 4.11 and following). See the linear-algebra appendix.

title: K-Means Clustering
text: Unsupervised · the workhorse for finding groups when you have no labels — partition the data into K clusters by minimizing within-cluster spread. Siblings: PCA (its natural partner — reduce dimensions/denoise then cluster, the exam pipeline), hierarchical clustering (groups without pre-setting K), and the supervised classifiers (LDA, logistic, trees) you should use instead the moment you actually have labels.

title: K-Means Clustering
text:
1. Essence
K-means partitions n observations into a pre-chosen number K of clusters so that points inside a cluster are as similar as possible and points in different clusters as dissimilar as possible (Lecture 6, slide 13/19). “Similar” means close in Euclidean distance, and the quantity it actually minimizes is the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS): the total squared distance from every point to the centroid of its assigned cluster. Each cluster is summarized by one point — its centroid \mu_i, the mean of the points assigned to it — and that centroid is precisely the location that minimizes squared distance to the cluster’s members (Lecture 6, slide 13/19). The output is a hard assignment: every point belongs to exactly one cluster, with no soft/probabilistic membership.
The algorithm alternates two cheap steps until the assignments stop changing: assign each point to its nearest centroid, then update each centroid to the mean of its newly assigned points (Lloyd’s algorithm). This always lowers WCSS and converges, but only to a local optimum — so the result depends on where the centroids started (Lecture 6, slide 15/19). Two standard guards address that fragility: k-means++ spreads the initial centroids out cleverly instead of picking them at random, and running the whole thing multiple times from different seeds (n_init) and keeping the lowest-WCSS solution. Both are on by default in scikit-learn.
The two design decisions that make or break a K-means analysis are choosing K and trusting the assumptions. K is not learned — you supply it — so the course teaches two tools to choose it: the Elbow method (plot WCSS against K and look for the kink where extra clusters stop paying off) and Silhouette analysis (a score in [-1,1] measuring how much better each point fits its own cluster than the next-nearest one). And K-means assumes spherical, roughly equal-sized clusters and is sensitive to outliers (a single far-flung point can drag a centroid toward it), because it is built on squared Euclidean distance (Lecture 6, slides 15/17). Compared with PCA — the other unsupervised method in this course — PCA re-describes the data along variance-maximizing axes (continuous, no groups), whereas K-means carves it into discrete groups; they combine beautifully, PCA first to denoise and shrink dimensions, K-means second to cluster (Lecture 6, slide 18/19).

title: K-Means Clustering
section: 2. When to use / when not to use
text:
2. When to use / when not to use

Reach for K-means when…

You have no labels and want to discover groups / segments — market or customer segmentation, document grouping, image-color quantization (Lecture 6, slide 16/19). The exam’s customer-segmentation task on WholesaleCustomers is exactly this (see §7).
You expect clusters that are roughly round and similar in size, and your features are continuous and on comparable scales (or you scale them first).
You want something fast and scalable — K-means is linear in n per iteration and handles large datasets where pairwise-distance methods choke.
You can pair it with PCA: reduce to a few components to denoise and visualize, then cluster — the course’s recommended combination (Lecture 6, slide 18/19).



Reach for something else when…

You actually have labels. Clustering ignores them; if the goal is to predict a known class, use a supervised model — LDA, logistic regression, decision trees. (The Iris example in §4 is a cautionary tale: the “best” K by silhouette is 2, not the 3 true species.)
Clusters are non-spherical, elongated, or very different in size / density → K-means’ equal-variance, round-blob assumption fails (Lecture 6, slide 17/19); reach for density- or shape-aware methods.
You don’t want to commit to K up front → hierarchical clustering builds a dendrogram you can cut at any level, no pre-set K required.
Outliers dominate → squared distance lets one stray point hijack a centroid (Lecture 6, slides 15/17); detect/trim outliers first, or use a robust alternative.
Features are wildly different in scale → the largest-unit feature dominates the Euclidean distance; standardize first (this is the most common K-means mistake, and the reason the exam pipeline scales before clustering — see §3).

title: K-Means Clustering
text:
3. Code idiom
The canonical course idiom is scikit-learn’s KMeans; the course does not build it from scratch — WCSS and the silhouette are introduced as formulas, and the clustering itself is always sklearn.cluster.KMeans (notebook 11_K_means.ipynb, cells 2, 8, 10).
Fit and read the labels (notebook 11_K_means.ipynb, cell 2):
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

# n_init = number of random restarts (best by WCSS is kept) — guards against bad init
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=3, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit(X)
kmeans.labels_            # hard cluster assignment (0..K-1) for each point
kmeans.cluster_centers_   # the K centroids μ_i
kmeans.inertia_           # the final WCSS (sum of squared point-to-centroid distances)
Every hyperparameter that matters: n_clusters is K, the number of clusters (no default worth relying on — you must choose it, see below); init defaults to 'k-means++' (smart spread-out initialization — leave it); n_init is how many restarts to run (the notebook uses 10); max_iter caps Lloyd iterations (default 300); random_state fixes the seed for reproducibility. The one attribute you will reuse constantly is .inertia_ — that is the WCSS, and it is what the elbow method plots.
Choosing K — elbow (WCSS) + silhouette, in one loop (notebook 11_K_means.ipynb, cell 8, verbatim):
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

wcss = []
silhouette_scores = []
for k in range(2, 10):
    kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, init='k-means++', max_iter=300, n_init=10, random_state=0)
    kmeans.fit(X)
    wcss.append(kmeans.inertia_)                              # elbow curve
    silhouette_scores.append(silhouette_score(X, kmeans.labels_))  # quality curve
WCSS (inertia_) always falls as K grows, so you look for the elbow — the kink where it stops falling fast. The silhouette, by contrast, has a genuine maximum: the K that scores highest is the silhouette’s pick. They do not always agree with each other, nor with any “true” number of groups — which is the whole lesson of §4.

Standardize before you cluster (unless features already share a scale). K-means uses raw Euclidean distance, so a feature measured in thousands (annual spend) will dominate one measured in single digits. The lecture stresses normalization as preprocessing (Lecture 6, slide 13/19 prose); the notebook skips it on Iris only because petal length and width are already both in centimetres on a similar range (notebook 11_K_means.ipynb, cell 1 advises normalization; cell 2 does not scale — petal features are pre-comparable). On any real multi-unit dataset (the exam’s WholesaleCustomers), fit a StandardScaler first — ideally inside the same scale → PCA → K-means pipeline (§4).

title: K-Means Clustering
text:
4. Worked examples

Example 1 — Iris elbow + silhouette, and why “best K” ≠ “3 species”
The course clusters Iris on just two features — petal length and petal width (notebook 11_K_means.ipynb, cell 2), deliberately ignoring the Species label (clustering is unsupervised). The silhouette is highest at K=2 (0.765), so the notebook’s next cell selects two clusters — and here is the catch worth quoting. The cell’s comment says one thing and the code does another:
# Apply k-means clustering with 3 clusters (one for each species of iris)
kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=2, random_state=0, n_init=10).fit(X)   # ← actually K=2
The comment is stale (copied from the earlier cell-2 that used n_clusters=3); the actual call is n_clusters=2 (notebook 11_K_means.ipynb, cell 10; see [disagreements NB-4]). This mismatch is a gift of a teaching point, not a bug to paper over: the silhouette-optimal K=2 is not the 3 true Iris species. On petal features, setosa sits in a tight, well-separated blob while versicolor and virginica overlap heavily — so two clusters (setosa vs. the-rest) score as “cleaner” than three. To see how the two choices compare against the (known, but withheld) species labels, score each clustering with the Adjusted Rand Index (computed via .venv):

K=3 recovers the species almost perfectly (ARI 0.886 — only 6 of 150 flowers land in the “wrong” cluster, all on the versicolor/virginica border), yet scores a lower silhouette than K=2 (computed). Lesson: the silhouette measures geometric separation, not correctness. With no labels you would have shipped K=2; the moment you have labels you would not be clustering at all. This is the single most important caveat about choosing K (see the big-picture callout in §6).


Example 2 — clustering with a ground truth: seeds
The local seeds.csv (140 grain samples, 7 geometric features, with a type variety label) lets us check clustering against a known answer — the “clustering with ground truth” case (course_materials/Data/seeds.csv; [DATA-2]). Crucially, this copy contains two wheat varieties (70 each), not the three of the full UCI set — so unlike Iris, the true count is 2. After StandardScaler (these features span very different units — area ~15, asymmetry ~2 — so scaling is mandatory), the elbow/silhouette loop gives (computed via .venv, random_state=0):
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(seeds.drop(columns=["type"]))   # 140 × 7, scaled
# same elbow/silhouette loop as §3 → silhouette peaks at K=2 (0.440)
The silhouette peaks at K=2 (0.440), falling to 0.299 at K=3 — and here the silhouette’s pick agrees with the ground truth. The K=2 clustering matches the two varieties well: ARI 0.758, with only 9 of 140 grains misassigned (computed). This is the happy mirror image of Iris: when the natural geometric grouping is the labelled grouping, silhouette and ground truth coincide. The contrast between the two examples — Iris (silhouette disagrees with labels) and seeds (silhouette agrees) — is exactly why you cannot treat the silhouette-optimal K as automatically “the right answer.”


Example 3 — the exam pipeline: scale → PCA → K-means on Wholesale customers
The Spring-2025 exam’s clustering task (Assignment 2) is customer segmentation on WholesaleCustomers.csv — 440 clients, 6 annual-spend categories (Fresh, Milk, Grocery, Frozen, Detergents_Paper, Delicassen) (course_materials/Lecture slides/Past exams/.../WholesaleCustomers.csv). The exam pipeline is standardize → PCA → K-means with elbow + silhouette to choose K — PCA both denoises and lets you visualize the clusters in 2-D:
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(wholesale[spend_cols])   # 6 spend features, scaled
Xp = PCA(n_components=2, random_state=0).fit_transform(X)    # project to PC1, PC2
# elbow/silhouette loop on Xp → choose K
On the scaled data, PCA needs 4 components for ≥90 % of the variance, while the first two alone capture 72.5 % — enough for a 2-D segmentation view (computed; cf. the PCA page and Asgmt 2’s “90 % variance” sub-task). Clustering on the PC1–PC2 projection, the silhouette is highest at K=2 (0.636), with K=3 a close second (0.627) and a clear elbow in WCSS around K=3–4 (WCSS: 1227.9, 891.0, 612.8, 427.2, … for K=2 \ldots 5; computed via .venv). The honest read: K=2 separates the two dominant buyer types (the Channel/Region columns, withheld from clustering, broadly correspond to Horeca vs. Retail), while K=3 is defensible from the elbow — a textbook case where elbow and silhouette nudge you toward different K and you justify the choice rather than read it off mechanically (§7).

5. Visualization
The figure that earns its place is the elbow + silhouette pair from Example 1 — it makes the entire K-selection decision visible at once. WCSS (left axis logic) only ever falls, so you hunt for the kink; the silhouette has a real peak. Plotting both on Iris’s petal features shows the tension at the heart of §4: the silhouette’s maximum sits at K=2, while the WCSS elbow and the true 3-species structure both point at K=3. title: K-Means Clustering
text:
6. Diagnostics & interpretation
What to report and inspect to judge a K-means clustering:

The elbow curve (WCSS vs K) — inertia_ for each K; pick the kink where the marginal drop flattens. It is a guide, not a rule: the elbow is often ambiguous (Wholesale’s sits between 3 and 4).
The silhouette curve (and per-cluster silhouettes) — the K with the highest mean silhouette is the silhouette’s pick; values near 1 mean tight, well-separated clusters, near 0 mean overlap, negative mean misassigned points. Inspect the per-cluster silhouette widths, not just the mean — one good cluster can mask one bad one.
Centroids and cluster sizes — read cluster_centers_ back in the original feature units to name the segments (“high-grocery, low-fresh” buyers); check that sizes aren’t wildly imbalanced (a tiny cluster may just be outliers).
Stability across restarts and seeds — because K-means finds only a local optimum, refit with several random_state values; assignments that flip a lot signal an ill-posed K or non-spherical structure.
Against any held-out labels (if they exist) — score with the Adjusted Rand Index, as in Examples 1–2. But remember: if you have labels, clustering was the wrong tool.


Elbow vs. silhouette vs. ground truth — the three can all disagree, and that’s the point. The elbow asks “where do extra clusters stop reducing spread?” (a within-cluster compactness question); the silhouette asks “how cleanly separated are the clusters?” (a between-vs-within question); the ground truth, when it exists, asks “do the clusters match the real categories?” On Iris these split three ways — silhouette says 2, elbow leans 3, truth is 3 — whereas on seeds all three agree on 2. There is no K-selection criterion that is always right, because clustering is an unsupervised judgement about structure, not a prediction with an answer key. And all of this presumes K-means’ core assumption — roughly spherical, equal-size clusters: when clusters are elongated, nested, or differ in density, every K-selection rule misleads, and the fix is a different algorithm, not a different K (Lecture 6, slide 17/19). Pair with PCA to denoise first, but heed the lecture’s caution — don’t reduce dimensions too much (slide 18/19).

title: K-Means Clustering
text:
7. Past-exam lens

How K-means shows up — this is core. In the Spring-2025 take-home (Assignment 2), K-means is the clustering half of an unsupervised pipeline on WholesaleCustomers.csv: standardize the spend features → PCA (including the “how many components for 90 % of variance” sub-task — the answer is 4; computed) → K-means, choosing K with the elbow method and silhouette analysis (§4). Expect to (i) write the KMeans(...).fit and silhouette_score idiom from §3 — with a StandardScaler first; (ii) run the elbow/silhouette loop over a range of K and plot both; (iii) choose and justify K — the graded skill is the reasoning when elbow and silhouette disagree (Wholesale: silhouette 2, elbow ~3), not a mechanical readout; and (iv) interpret the segments by reading the centroids back in spend units. The classic trap: forgetting to scale, so Fresh/Grocery (thousands) swamp the distance and the clusters become meaningless. The Iris caveat from §4 is the conceptual point examiners love — optimal K need not equal the number of true classes.

title: K-Means Clustering
text:
8. Math


Math is off. Use the Math toggle in the top bar to show the course-level derivation (and “full” for the rigorous version).


Mode A — course level. (Notation: K = number of clusters, S_i = the i-th cluster (a set of points), \mu_i = its centroid; this K/S_i/μ_i convention follows Lecture 6 — see notation table.) The course poses K-means as a single optimization, the within-cluster sum of squares (WCSS). Partition the data into clusters \{S_1,\dots,S_K\} to \min_{S_1,\dots,S_K}\;\sum_{i=1}^{K}\sum_{x\in S_i}\lVert x-\mu_i\rVert^2, where \mu_i=\frac{1}{|S_i|}\sum_{x\in S_i}x is the centroid (mean) of cluster S_i — defined on the slide as “the point in feature space minimizing squared distance to all points in its cluster” (Lecture 6, slides 13–14/19). This objective is exactly scikit-learn’s inertia_ (§3). Reading it: \lVert x-\mu_i\rVert^2 is squared Euclidean distance, so WCSS is the total squared spread of points around their cluster’s center; minimizing it makes within-cluster points as similar, and between-cluster points as dissimilar, as possible.
The course does not solve this in closed form — there is none. Instead it runs Lloyd’s algorithm, which alternates two cheap steps until the assignments stop changing: (a) assign each point to its nearest centroid (Euclidean distance), then (b) update each centroid to the mean of its newly assigned points. Each pass lowers WCSS, so it converges — but only to a local optimum that depends on the initial centroids (Lecture 6, slide 15/19). The course’s two guards against bad initializations: k-means++ seeds the starting centroids spread out (each new seed drawn with probability proportional to its squared distance to the nearest existing centroid — init='k-means++', the sklearn default), and multiple restarts (n_init, the notebook uses 10) keep the lowest-WCSS run (Lecture 6, slide 15/19; notebook 11_K_means.ipynb, cell 8). The full local-vs-global / convergence argument is in Mode B. See the math appendix.


Mode B — full rigor. (Anchored to ISL §12.4.1, eqs 12.15–12.18, and ESL §14.3.6, eqs 14.31–14.34.)
The pairwise form and why it equals the centroid form. ISL frames K-means as minimizing the total within-cluster variation, \operatorname*{minimize}_{C_1,\dots,C_K}\;\Bigl\{\sum_{k=1}^{K} W(C_k)\Bigr\}\qquad\text{(ISL 12.15),} and takes the most common choice of W(C_k) — the mean pairwise squared Euclidean distance inside a cluster, W(C_k)=\frac{1}{|C_k|}\sum_{i,i'\in C_k}\sum_{j=1}^{p}\bigl(x_{ij}-x_{i'j}\bigr)^2\qquad\text{(ISL 12.16).} This pairwise bookkeeping never names a centroid, yet ISL’s key identity (12.18) shows it is the same objective as the slide’s centroid form: \frac{1}{|C_k|}\sum_{i,i'\in C_k}\sum_{j}\bigl(x_{ij}-x_{i'j}\bigr)^2 \;=\; 2\sum_{i\in C_k}\sum_{j}\bigl(x_{ij}-\bar x_{kj}\bigr)^2\qquad\text{(ISL 12.18),} where \bar x_{kj}=\tfrac{1}{|C_k|}\sum_{i\in C_k}x_{ij} is the cluster mean — i.e. the centroid \mu_k. So ISL’s pairwise W(C_k) equals twice the slide’s per-cluster centroid sum \sum_{i\in C_k}\lVert x_i-\mu_k\rVert^2: the two forms have the same minimizer and differ only by the constant factor 2 in this normalization ([disagreements R9-4]; the slide/centroid form is primary here because it is what inertia_ computes). ESL writes the same equivalence with the cluster size N_k=|C_k| made explicit (ESL 14.31): the within-point scatter W(C)=\tfrac12\sum_k\sum_{C(i)=k}\sum_{C(i')=k}\lVert x_i-x_{i'}\rVert^2=\sum_{k}N_k\sum_{C(i)=k}\lVert x_i-\bar x_k\rVert^2.
Why Lloyd’s algorithm decreases WCSS — and only to a local optimum. ESL’s identity (14.32) is the engine: for any set of points S, \;\bar x_S=\arg\min_m\sum_{i\in S}\lVert x_i-m\rVert^2 — the mean is the unique minimizer of summed squared distance. This lets the joint problem be written over both assignments C and centers \{m_k\}, \min_{C,\{m_k\}}\;\sum_{k=1}^{K}N_k\sum_{C(i)=k}\lVert x_i-m_k\rVert^2\qquad\text{(ESL 14.33),} and minimized by alternating (Algorithm 14.1): (a) hold C fixed, set each m_k=\bar x_k (optimal by 14.32); (b) hold \{m_k\} fixed, reassign C(i)=\arg\min_{1\le k\le K}\lVert x_i-m_k\rVert^2 (ESL 14.34). This is coordinate descent: each step minimizes (14.33) over one block with the other fixed, so “each of steps 1 and 2 reduces the value of the criterion (14.33), so that convergence is assured” (ESL §14.3.6). But it is descent on a non-convex surface — the objective never increases, yet “the result may represent a suboptimal local minimum” depending on the random start (ESL §14.3.6). ISL makes the combinatorial source of the difficulty concrete: there are “almost K^n ways to partition n observations into K clusters … a very difficult problem to solve precisely,” so Lloyd’s algorithm only “provides a local optimum — a pretty good solution” (ISL §12.4.1, around eq 12.17). This is exactly why both texts insist on multiple random restarts, keeping the run with the smallest objective (ESL §14.3.6; ISL §12.4.1, where six restarts find objectives ranging 235.8–320.9 and the best is chosen) — and why scikit-learn defaults to k-means++ plus n_init restarts (§3).
The implicit isotropic-Gaussian model. ESL §14.3.7 (“Gaussian Mixtures as Soft K-means”) shows K-means is the hard limit of fitting a mixture of Gaussians with scalar covariance \sigma^2\mathbf I: the EM “responsibilities” become 0/1 assignments as \sigma^2\to0, and the two methods coincide (ESL §14.3.7). That is the precise sense in which K-means assumes spherical, equal-variance clusters — the round-blob assumption flagged in §2 and §6 is not a heuristic but this isotropic-Gaussian model in disguise. It also explains the natural pairing with PCA: projecting onto variance-maximizing axes first denoises and reshapes the data toward the spherical geometry K-means expects (Lecture 6, slide 18/19), and ties choosing K to the bias–variance view — larger K always lowers WCSS (less bias) but eventually carves noise, which is why the elbow/silhouette judgement of §4 cannot be read off the objective alone. See the math appendix.

title: Decision Trees
text: Tree family · the interpretable non-parametric classifier that splits the feature space into axis-aligned boxes — and the high-variance building block every ensemble is made of. Siblings: Random Forests and Ensembles (average / boost many trees to tame the variance), Logistic Regression and LDA (linear boundaries instead of axis-aligned cuts), kNN (the other non-parametric local learner).

title: Decision Trees
text:
1. Essence
A decision tree predicts by asking a sequence of simple yes/no questions about one feature at a time — “is petal width ≤ 0.8?”, then “is petal length ≤ 4.95?” — until it reaches a leaf, where it returns the majority class of the training points that landed there. It is built by recursively partitioning the training set: starting from the whole sample at the root, the algorithm searches every feature and every candidate threshold, picks the single split that makes the two resulting subsets as pure (class-homogeneous) as possible, and then repeats the same procedure on each subset until a stopping rule fires (Lecture 4, slides 9–10/11). The result is a flowchart you can read top-to-bottom, which is the method’s headline selling point.
It is a non-parametric model: it commits to no functional form and no fixed number of parameters, so it can carve out arbitrarily complex, axis-aligned decision regions and capture non-linearities and interactions automatically — no scaling, no encoding, no linearity assumption (Lecture 4, slide 9/11). That flexibility is also its weakness. Grown unchecked, a tree will keep splitting until every leaf is pure, memorizing the training data; and because each split depends on the one above it, a tiny change in the data can flip an early split and reshape the whole tree — trees are high-variance and unstable (Lecture 4, slide 9/11; Lecture 7, slide 15/21).
Compared with its nearest neighbors: a single tree is the baseline that Random Forests and Ensembles exist to improve on — they grow many trees and average (bagging) or stage (boosting) them to cancel out that variance. Against the linear classifiers, a tree draws staircase boundaries (perpendicular cuts) where Logistic Regression and LDA draw a single straight line — a tree wins when the true boundary is blocky or interaction-heavy, and loses (needing a deep, jagged staircase) when it is genuinely linear. Like kNN it is non-parametric and makes local decisions, but a tree’s regions are learned splits rather than distance to stored points.

title: Decision Trees
section: 2. When to use / when not to use
text:
2. When to use / when not to use

Reach for a decision tree when…

You want a fully interpretable model you can read as a flowchart and show a non-technical stakeholder — the path from root to leaf is the explanation (Lecture 4, slide 9/11).
Features are a mix of types and scales (numeric, ordinal, categorical) and you’d rather not standardize or one-hot-encode — trees split on thresholds, so no feature scaling is needed (Lecture 4, slide 9/11).
The relationship is non-linear with interactions and you don’t want to hand-engineer terms — recursive splitting captures curvature and “feature A matters only when feature B is high” for free.
You need a fast, transparent baseline before reaching for the heavier machinery. On the Spring-2025 exam’s breast-cancer task (Assignment 3), a single tree is exactly that baseline before Random Forests and gradient boosting (see §7).



Reach for something else when…

Predictive accuracy and stability matter more than reading a single tree → a lone tree overfits and is high-variance. Bag it into a Random Forest or stage it with gradient boosting — that is the entire reason those methods exist, and exactly the progression the exam asks for (§7). The depth curve in §5 shows the overfitting symptom directly.
The true boundary is essentially linear → Logistic Regression or LDA capture it with one smooth boundary, whereas a tree needs a deep, jagged staircase of axis-aligned cuts to approximate a diagonal line (and overfits doing so).
The data is small and noisy → tree structure is unstable; a few flipped points can rebuild the tree (Lecture 7, slide 15/21). Prefer a lower-variance model or, again, an ensemble.
You need smooth probability estimates or “+1 unit ⇒ +β” effect sizes → a tree’s leaf probabilities are piecewise-constant and coarse; use a linear model for calibrated, interpretable coefficients.

title: Decision Trees
text:
3. Code idiom
The canonical course idiom is scikit-learn’s DecisionTreeClassifier from sklearn.tree, paired with plot_tree to render the flowchart. The course uses sklearn only here — there is no from-scratch tree in the lecture notebooks.
The default tree — fit, score, inspect size (notebook 07_Decision_trees.ipynb, cell 7):
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)

clf = DecisionTreeClassifier()        # all defaults: criterion='gini', max_depth=None (grow until pure)
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
clf.score(X_test, y_test)             # accuracy on the held-out 30%
clf.get_depth(); clf.get_n_leaves()   # how big did the unconstrained tree grow?
Choosing the split criterion, and pre-pruning to fight overfitting (notebook 07_Decision_trees.ipynb, cells 12, 13, 16):
DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion='gini',    random_state=0)   # default criterion (Gini impurity)
DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion='entropy', random_state=0)   # entropy ≡ information gain

# Pre-pruning: require ≥5 training samples in every leaf → shallower, simpler tree
clf_pruned = DecisionTreeClassifier(min_samples_leaf=5, random_state=0)
clf_pruned.fit(X_train, y_train)
Every hyperparameter, annotated. criterion selects the impurity measure — 'gini' is the default (slightly cheaper to compute), 'entropy' uses information gain (§8; the two usually give very similar trees). random_state fixes the tie-breaking among equally-good splits, so set it for reproducibility. The stopping / pre-pruning knobs all default to “grow until pure”: max_depth=None (no depth cap), min_samples_split=2, min_samples_leaf=1, min_impurity_decrease=0.0. Tightening any of them — e.g. max_depth=3 or min_samples_leaf=5 — shrinks the tree and trades a little training fit for lower variance. In practice you tune these by cross-validation (GridSearchCV), which is exactly what the exam’s Assignment 3.3 asks for (§7).

A default tree overfits — and watch the leaf-count comment trap. With max_depth=None the tree splits until every leaf is pure, so training accuracy goes to 100% while test accuracy peaks early and then sags (the §5 depth curve shows this on real WDBC data). Always pre-prune (max_depth / min_samples_leaf) or, better, ensemble. Two implementation traps from notebook 07 worth flagging so you don’t copy them blindly: (i) cell 17 builds the “pruned” tree with min_samples_leaf=10 even though the surrounding comment and the plot title both say “5” — quote the actual value 10 if you lift it [NB-1]; (ii) cells 12, 13 and 17 fit on the full X, y (for a complete-looking picture) rather than on X_train — only cells 7 and 16 use the train/test split, so don’t read those full-data trees as held-out evaluations [NB-1].

title: Decision Trees
text:
4. Worked examples

Example 1 — a default tree on Iris, and the size it grows to
The course’s running example is the Iris dataset (150 flowers, 3 species, 4 features), loaded from the UCI URL with a 70/30 split (random_state=0) (notebook 07_Decision_trees.ipynb, cells 4, 7). An unconstrained DecisionTreeClassifier() fit on the 105 training flowers:
clf = DecisionTreeClassifier().fit(X_train, y_train)
clf.score(X_test, y_test)   # 0.9778
clf.get_depth()             # 4
clf.get_n_leaves()          # 7
scores test accuracy ≈ 0.978 (44/45 correct) with a tree of depth 4 and 7 leaves (computed via the course .venv, reproducing nb07 cell 7; random_state=0). Iris is nearly linearly separable on petal measurements, so even a default tree generalizes well — but note it still grew to 7 leaves on 105 points, fitting some of the training-set detail it didn’t need. The tree’s feature_importances_ confirm the intuition: petal_width carries ≈ 0.92 of the importance and sepal_length exactly 0.0 — the tree never splits on it (computed). That is decision-tree feature selection happening for free, and the kind of ranking Assignment 3.7 asks for on the breast-cancer data.


Example 2 — Gini vs entropy, and pre-pruning the tree
Re-fitting with each split criterion (notebook cells 12, 13) — both on the same data — produces trees of identical size: depth 5, 9 leaves for Gini and for entropy (computed via .venv). This is the practical face of disagreement R9-1: Gini and (log₂) entropy are different formulas but rank candidate splits almost identically, so they usually yield the same tree — the course notebook says as much (“both often yield similar results, although gini is somewhat faster”, nb07 cell 2).
Now pre-prune. Requiring at least 5 samples per leaf (notebook cell 16, on the train split) collapses the tree from depth 4 to depth 3 with 5 leaves, but here test accuracy drops to 0.911 (computed) — on an already-easy problem, pruning bought simplicity at a small accuracy cost rather than a gain. (The notebook’s next cell, 17, then builds a tree with min_samples_leaf=10 fit on the full X, y — depth 4, 6 leaves — and mislabels it “min_samples_leaf=5”; that is the [NB-1] code/comment mismatch from §3, and the depth-4 figure is over the whole dataset, not a held-out score.) The lesson: pruning is a variance-reducing move — it earns its keep when the unpruned tree is overfitting, which Iris barely does but WDBC clearly does (Example 3).


Example 3 — a single tree as the WDBC baseline (exam Assignment 3)
The Spring-2025 exam’s Assignment 3 classifies the Wisconsin Diagnostic Breast Cancer data (wdbc.data: 569 tumors, 30 real-valued nucleus features, target malignant M / benign B, 357 B / 212 M) and walks up the tree family: single tree → Random Forest → gradient boosting (phase0/exam_spring2025_notebook.md). The single tree is step 3.3 — the baseline the ensembles must beat. With a stratified 75/25 split (random_state=1):
df = pd.read_csv("wdbc.data", header=None)        # col 1 = diagnosis, cols 2: = 30 features
X, y = df.iloc[:, 2:].values, df[1].values
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=1)

tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=1).fit(Xtr, ytr)
tree.score(Xtr, ytr)   # 1.000  ← memorized the training set
tree.score(Xte, yte)   # 0.923
An unconstrained tree hits train accuracy 1.000 but test accuracy 0.923 (depth 7, 18 leaves) — the train–test gap is the overfitting fingerprint in plain sight (computed via .venv). Tuning the complexity by 5-fold cross-validation (Assignment 3.3) selects max_depth=5 with CV accuracy ≈ 0.944 and test accuracy ≈ 0.909 — barely different on the test set, because a single tree’s variance can’t be cross-validated away, only ensembled away (computed). That is precisely why the exam continues to Random Forests and boosting (3.4–3.6): the §5 depth curve shows the test accuracy plateauing around 0.92 no matter how deep you grow, while a forest of such trees pushes it higher.

This is the setup where Random Forests and Ensembles earn their keep, and why the exam pairs the single tree with them: a tree is a high-variance, low-bias learner, so averaging many decorrelated trees (bagging / RF) slashes the variance at almost no bias cost. See the classification showdown for Tree vs RF vs Gradient Boosting on this same WDBC data.

title: Decision Trees
text:
5. Visualization
The one figure that earns its place for a decision tree is the overfitting curve: training and test accuracy as the tree is allowed to grow deeper. It makes the family’s defining failure mode visible — training accuracy climbs monotonically to a perfect 1.0 as the tree memorizes, while test accuracy peaks early and then stops improving (here it plateaus; on noisier data it would decline). The gap that opens between the two lines is the variance that Random Forests and Ensembles are built to close. The data below is computed on the real WDBC exam dataset (75/25 stratified split, random_state=1).

The green line is training accuracy — it climbs straight to 1.0 by depth 7 as the tree memorizes the 426 training tumors. The grey line is test accuracy — it peaks at depth 2–3 (≈0.93) and then plateaus around 0.92 no matter how much deeper the tree grows. The widening gap between the two lines is the tree’s variance: extra depth buys training fit but not generalization. This is exactly why the exam moves on to Random Forests and boosting.
