title: Ensemble Methods
text:
6. Diagnostics & interpretation
What to report and inspect to judge an ensemble:

Ensemble vs base-learner accuracy — always report the single base model alongside the ensemble (single tree 0.9386 vs bagged ≥ 0.943 above). If the ensemble does not beat its base learner, it is not earning its complexity.
Out-of-bag (OOB) error — bagging gives a free hold-out: each model never saw ~37% of the data (the ~63% bootstrap fact, §8), so the OOB predictions estimate test error without a separate split. (BaggingClassifier(oob_score=True).)
The n_estimators curve — for bagging, test error should fall then plateau as you add models (more trees rarely hurt); for boosting, it can fall then rise (boosting can overfit), so the curve is a genuine stopping-criterion diagnostic, tuned together with the learning rate \eta (Lecture 7, slides 11–12/21).
Feature importances — ensembles of trees expose feature_importances_ for ranking drivers — but note the notebook plots the single tree’s importances (cell 14), not the ensemble’s. Importances rank features; unlike OLS coefficients they give no signed “+1 unit ⇒ +β” reading.
ROC AUC — the metric the income exercise specifies for the boosted model (cell 5); appropriate for the imbalanced income target.


Bagging vs boosting vs stacking — the choice in one breath. Bagging (parallel, bootstrap, average) attacks variance — use it when a high-variance learner like a deep tree overfits; Random Forests are the go-to instance. Boosting (sequential, reweight the misclassified, learning rate \eta) attacks bias — use it to turn weak learners into a strong one, watching for overfitting. Stacking learns a meta-model over diverse base models — the most flexible and the most prone to overfit. Across all three you are spending interpretability for performance (Lecture 7, slide 3/21): the gain is real, but you lose the single readable model that OLS or a lone decision tree gives you. Decision rule: train–test gap ⇒ bagging; underfitting ⇒ boosting; several good diverse models to fuse ⇒ stacking.

title: Ensemble Methods
text:
7. Past-exam lens

How ensembles show up. In the take-home Assignment 3 (on WDBC / breast cancer), ensembles are central: the assignment uses gradient boosting and explicitly asks you to compare a Random Forest against gradient boosting (task 3.8) — i.e. bagging vs boosting on the same data. Expect to (i) write the GradientBoostingClassifier idiom from §3, (ii) tune n_estimators / learning_rate (\eta) / max_depth and justify the values, (iii) report and interpret performance (the income exercise’s ROC AUC is the same skill on a different dataset, §4 Example 3), and (iv) explain the RF-vs-GB difference in terms of variance reduction vs bias reduction — the §6 big-picture callout is the answer template. The grade rests on the reasoning (why one ensemble suits the data) at least as much as the code. The classic slip: confusing the boosting learning rate \eta (learning_rate) with the number of trees — they trade off (smaller \eta ⇒ more trees).

title: Ensemble Methods
text:
8. Math


Math is off. Use the Math toggle in the top bar to show the course-level derivation (and “full” for the rigorous version).


Mode A — course level. The course states the two combination rules and the bootstrap fact procedurally — there are no boosting formulas on the Lecture 7 slides (see Mode B for those). (Symbols: B = number of base models, n = sample size, \eta = boosting learning rate — notation_table η.)
Bagging. Train B base models \hat f_1,\dots,\hat f_B, each on a separate bootstrap resample, then combine. For regression, average them, \hat f_{\text{bag}}(x)=\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^{B}\hat f_b(x); for classification, take the majority vote of the B predicted labels (Lecture 7, slides 6/21, 9/21; notebook 12_..., cells 5–6). Averaging many noisy-but-unbiased models cancels their independent errors, so bagging reduces variance (Lecture 7, slide 6/21).
Boosting. The slides give the procedure, not an equation (Lecture 7, slide 12/21): (1) initialise equal example weights w_i=\tfrac1n; (2) train a weak learner on the weighted data; (3) evaluate it; (4) increase the weights of misclassified examples and decrease the rest; (5) repeat to a stopping criterion; (6) the final prediction is a weighted combination of all weak learners, with the learning rate \eta scaling each one’s contribution (smaller \eta ⇒ each tree counts for less, usually needing more trees). Concentrating successive learners on the hard cases reduces bias (Lecture 7, slide 11/21).
Bootstrap. Resampling n points with replacement from n, any one point is missed by a single draw with probability (1-1/n)^n, so about 63% of the unique original samples appear in each bootstrap sample (Lecture 7, slide 7/21). The ~37% omitted form a free hold-out — the out-of-bag (OOB) estimate. The exact 0.632 limit is derived in Mode B ([disagreements R9-6]). See the math appendix.


Mode B — full rigor. Everything below is supplemental: it is not on the Lecture 7 slides, which describe boosting and the bootstrap only procedurally ([disagreements R9-8, R9-6]). It is anchored to ESL §10.1–10.4 (AdaBoost) and §7.11 (bootstrap), with equation numbers read directly from the text.
AdaBoost.M1 (ESL Algorithm 10.1, §10.1). For a two-class target y_i\in\{-1,1\} and weak classifiers G_m(x)\in\{-1,1\}: initialise weights w_i=1/N; for m=1,\dots,M, fit G_m to the data weighted by w_i, compute the weighted error \mathrm{err}_m=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i\,I\big(y_i\neq G_m(x_i)\big)}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} w_i}, set the stage weight \alpha_m=\log\frac{1-\mathrm{err}_m}{\mathrm{err}_m}\qquad\text{(ESL Alg. 10.1, line 2c — note }\log,\text{ no }\tfrac12), and reweight w_i\leftarrow w_i\cdot\exp\!\big[\alpha_m\,I(y_i\neq G_m(x_i))\big]. The final classifier is the weighted vote G(x)=\operatorname{sign}\!\big[\sum_{m=1}^{M}\alpha_m G_m(x)\big] (ESL 10.1). A more accurate stage (small \mathrm{err}_m) earns a larger \alpha_m, hence more vote.
Why the \tfrac12 sometimes appears. AdaBoost.M1 is equivalent to forward stagewise additive modeling (ESL Algorithm 10.2, §10.3) — building f_m(x)=f_{m-1}(x)+\beta_m b(x;\gamma_m) one basis function at a time — on the exponential loss L(y,f)=\exp(-y\,f(x)) (ESL 10.8, §10.4). Minimising that loss at step m first selects G_m as the weighted-error minimiser (ESL 10.10–10.11), then solves for the coefficient \beta_m=\tfrac12\log\frac{1-\mathrm{err}_m}{\mathrm{err}_m}\qquad\text{(ESL 10.12).} The algorithm’s stage weight is exactly \alpha_m=2\beta_m (ESL §10.4, after eq 10.15) — the \tfrac12 is absorbed because the \{-1,1\} reweighting only depends on \alpha_m. So the ½ belongs to the exponential-loss derivation, while the plain \log is the form used inside the AdaBoost.M1 algorithm itself.
Gradient / least-squares boosting (ESL §10.3–10.4). With squared-error loss L(y,f)=(y-f)^2 (ESL 10.6), the forward-stagewise subproblem reduces to fitting each new basis function to the current residuals: with r_{im}=y_i-f_{m-1}(x_i), L\big(y_i,\,f_{m-1}(x_i)+\beta\,b(x_i;\gamma)\big)=\big(r_{im}-\beta\,b(x_i;\gamma)\big)^2\qquad\text{(ESL 10.7),} so \beta_m b(x;\gamma_m) best fits the residuals at each step. Generalising, each new learner is fit to the negative gradient of the loss at the current ensemble — boosting as gradient descent in function space — and the update f_m=f_{m-1}+\eta\,\beta_m b(x;\gamma_m) carries the same learning rate \eta (“slow learning”/shrinkage, ESL §10.12) as Mode A’s slides.
The 0.632 bootstrap (ESL §7.11). The probability that observation i is included in a given bootstrap sample is \Pr\{i\in \text{bootstrap sample}\}=1-\Big(1-\tfrac1N\Big)^{N}\;\xrightarrow{\,N\to\infty\,}\;1-e^{-1}\approx 0.632\qquad\text{(ESL 7.55),} so the expected number of distinct observations per draw is about 0.632\,N — the exact form of the slide’s “~63%” ([disagreements R9-6]). This constant names the “.632” estimator that corrects the optimism of training error, \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(.632)}=.368\cdot\overline{\mathrm{err}}+.632\cdot\widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(1)} (ESL 7.57), where \widehat{\mathrm{Err}}^{(1)} is the leave-one-out bootstrap error.
Bias–variance link. Bagging targets the variance term and boosting the bias term of the prediction-error decomposition; rather than re-derive it here, see the bias–variance decomposition in the math appendix. See also the math appendix.

title: k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN)
text: Linear family · the simplest possible supervised baseline — it stores the training set and classifies a new point by looking at who its neighbors are. Grouped here with the baseline supervised methods, but unlike the rest of the family it is non-parametric: it assumes no functional form at all. Siblings: Logistic Regression and LDA (parametric linear boundaries), Decision Trees (non-parametric, axis-aligned), OLS (the parametric regressor it is most often contrasted with).

title: k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN)
text:
1. Essence
k-Nearest Neighbors classifies a new point by a vote of its closest training examples: measure the distance from the query to every training point, keep the K nearest, and assign the label that the majority of those K hold (Lecture 2, slide 8/10). There is no “model” in the usual sense — nothing is fitted, no coefficients are estimated. The training set is the model; “fitting” just stores it. All the work happens at prediction time, when the distances are computed.
It is the textbook non-parametric method: it commits to no functional form and has no fixed number of parameters — the effective complexity grows with the data (Lecture 2, slide 9/10). That makes it flexible (it can carve out arbitrarily wiggly decision boundaries) and almost assumption-free, but also hungry for data, expensive to query, and exquisitely sensitive to two choices: how many neighbors to consult (K) and how distance is measured (the metric, and therefore the scale of the features).
The single knob, K, is the bias–variance dial made tangible. K too small → the boundary chases individual points → overfit, high variance. K too large → the vote washes out local structure toward the global majority → underfit, high bias (Lecture 2, slide 8/10). The course’s prescription is to choose K by cross-validation (Lecture 2, slide 8/10).
Compared with its nearest neighbors: OLS and logistic regression fix a form (a line/plane) and spend training time estimating a handful of coefficients, then predict instantly; kNN inverts that — instant “training,” expensive prediction, and a boundary that is local rather than global. Decision trees are the other non-parametric baseline, but they partition the space with axis-aligned cuts and ignore feature scale, whereas kNN measures raw distance and so demands that features be scaled.

title: k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN)
section: 2. When to use / when not to use
text:
2. When to use / when not to use

Reach for kNN when…

You want a fast-to-stand-up, assumption-free baseline for classification (it also does regression by averaging neighbors, Lecture 2 slide 8/10, but the course uses it as a classifier). It is the “first model” you try alongside Naive Bayes (Lecture 2, slide 8/10).
The decision boundary is irregular but locally smooth — kNN follows curvature that OLS/logistic cannot, without you specifying any form.
You have enough data relative to the number of features, and you can scale the features so distance is meaningful.
You want intuition you can point at: a prediction is literally “these K labeled examples nearby.”



Reach for something else when…

The feature space is high-dimensional → the curse of dimensionality makes “nearest” almost meaningless (all points become roughly equidistant). Use a parametric model (logistic/LDA), reduce dimensions first with PCA, or use a tree/random forest that selects features.
You need an interpretable global rule (“+1 unit of X ⇒ +β”) → kNN gives no coefficients; reach for OLS/logistic, or a decision tree for if-then rules.
Prediction must be cheap or the dataset is large → every query scans (a structure over) the whole training set; a fitted logistic or tree predicts in constant time (Lecture 2, slide 8/10: “computationally expensive for large data”).
Features are on wildly different scales and you can’t scale them → the largest-range feature silently dominates the distance (see §3 and the wine example in §4).
The boundary really is linear → a parametric linear model will match kNN with far less data and a readable boundary; this is the parametric-vs-non-parametric trade-off (Lecture 2, slide 9/10).

title: k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN)
text:
3. Code idiom
The course teaches kNN both from scratch (so the distance-and-vote mechanics are not a black box) and via scikit-learn’s KNeighborsClassifier. Both run on the same iris split with K = 3 and agree (§4).
Canonical (sklearn) — (notebook 03_Supervised_learning_with_kNN (1).ipynb, cell 12)
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

# Create a k-NN classifier with 3 neighbors
knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3)   # n_neighbors = K, the only knob you must set
knn.fit(X_train, y_train)                     # "fit" just stores the training data
y_pred = knn.predict(X_test)                  # the work happens here, at predict time
knn.score(X_test, y_test)                     # mean accuracy on the test set
n_neighbors (the K of the algorithm) is the hyperparameter you tune — by cross-validation, per Lecture 2 slide 8/10. Everything else in the notebook is left at the sklearn default: weights='uniform' (every neighbor votes equally — 'distance' would weight closer points more), and metric='minkowski' with p=2, which is Euclidean distance — exactly the metric the course defines (notebook cell 3).
From scratch — distance, sort, vote (notebook 03_Supervised_learning_with_kNN (1).ipynb, cell 7). This is the whole algorithm in three small functions, and shows literally what predict does under the hood — compute every distance, take the K smallest, majority-vote:
import numpy as np

def euclidean_distance(x, y):
    """Calculate the euclidean distance between two points"""
    return np.sqrt(np.sum((x - y)**2))

def predict(X_train, y_train, X_test, k):
    """Find the k nearest neighbors of x_test in X_train"""
    distances = [euclidean_distance(X_test, x) for x in X_train]  # distance to every train point
    k_nearest = np.argsort(distances)[:k]                          # indices of the K smallest
    return y_train[k_nearest]                                      # their labels

def predict_label(X_train, y_train, X_test, k):
    """Find the most common label among the k nearest neighbors of X_test in X_train"""
    return np.bincount(predict(X_train, y_train, X_test, k)).argmax()  # majority vote
Used across the whole test set with k = 3 (cell 8):
y_pred = [predict_label(X_train, y_train, x, 3) for x in X_test]
accuracy = np.mean(y_pred == y_test)

Scaling is not optional for kNN. Distance treats every feature in its raw units, so a feature with a large numeric range dominates the vote regardless of how informative it is. The course notebook feeds unscaled iris features straight in (cell 4 — no StandardScaler), which is fine only because iris’s four features share a comparable scale (all cm). On a dataset with mismatched ranges it silently breaks: on wine, proline (std ≈ 314) swamps features with std ≈ 0.12, and raw-feature kNN scores 68.89% versus 97.78% once standardized (§4, computed). Wrap kNN in a Pipeline([StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(...)]). (bincount in the from-scratch version also assumes non-negative integer labels — fine for iris targets {0,1,2}, but it would break on string labels.)

title: k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN)
text:
4. Worked examples

Example 1 — iris, from scratch vs sklearn (the cross-check)
The course’s anchor example loads iris, splits 80/20, and runs kNN both ways on the same split so the two implementations can be checked against each other (notebook 03_Supervised_learning_with_kNN (1).ipynb, cells 4, 8, 12):
from sklearn import datasets
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

iris = datasets.load_iris()
X, y = iris.data, iris.target                       # 150 × 4 features, 3 species
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=10)          # 120 train, 30 test
With K = 3 on this fixed split (random_state=10), the from-scratch classifier and KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3) both score 96.67% on the 30-point test set (29/30 correct) — they agree exactly, which is the point of the cross-check (computed; the notebook stores no outputs for cells 8/12). The single test point inspected first (cell 7) has true label 1 and is predicted 1 (computed). Iris is nearly linearly separable, so even this minimal classifier with no scaling does well.


Example 2 — choosing K is choosing your place on the bias–variance dial
Sweeping K on the same iris split makes the bias–variance trade-off concrete (computed, random_state=10):



K
train accuracy
test accuracy

100.00%

3

At K = 1 the training accuracy is a perfect 100% — every point is its own nearest neighbor — the textbook signature of high variance (it has memorized the training set). As K grows, the vote averages over a wider neighborhood; by K = 100 (out of only 120 training points) the model is essentially predicting the global majority class and collapses to 60% on test — textbook high bias / underfit (Lecture 2, slide 8/10). The sweet spot is in between, and you don’t read it off the test set — you pick it by cross-validation on the training data (5-fold CV here is flat at ≈ 94% for K = 3…25, computed; iris is too easy to produce a sharp optimum). The principle generalizes: small K overfits, large K underfits, choose K by CV (Lecture 2, slide 8/10).


Example 3 — why scaling decides the outcome (wine)
To show the scaling pitfall from §3 with numbers, take wine (13 chemical features on very different scales) with a 75/25 split (random_state=1), K = 3 (computed):
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

raw    = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3).fit(Xtr, ytr).score(Xte, yte)        # 0.6889
scaled = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3)
                       ).fit(Xtr, ytr).score(Xte, yte)                            # 0.9778
Raw-feature kNN gets 68.89%; standardizing first lifts it to 97.78% — a 29-point jump from one preprocessing line. The reason is mechanical: proline ranges in the hundreds-to-thousands (std ≈ 314) while other features sit near std ≈ 0.12, so before scaling the Euclidean distance is almost entirely the proline difference and the other twelve features barely vote. This is exactly why the Spring-2025 exam’s Assignment 4 explicitly asks you to “scale if necessary” and notes that “distance/gradient models like k-NN” need it, while trees do not (§7).

title: k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN)
k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN)
text:
6. Diagnostics & interpretation
What to look at to decide whether a kNN model is working:

Accuracy on a held-out set, and beyond accuracy — report precision, recall, F1 when classes are imbalanced (the Spring-2025 exam insists on this for Assignment 4, §7). A confusion matrix shows which classes the neighbors confuse.
The K curve (train vs CV accuracy across K) — the diagnostic that locates your bias–variance position (Example 2). A huge train–CV gap at small K signals variance; both sagging at large K signals bias. Pick K at the CV peak, never on the test set.
Did you scale? — the first thing to check on any disappointing kNN result. An unscaled distance-based model is the most common silent failure (Example 3): inspect feature ranges/standard deviations.
Dimensionality — as features multiply, “nearest” loses meaning (the curse of dimensionality, §8 Mode B). If accuracy degrades as you add features, that is the symptom; reduce with PCA or switch to a feature-selecting model.
Predict-time cost — there are no coefficients to read; a kNN “explanation” is the neighbor set itself. Watch query latency on large training sets (Lecture 2, slide 8/10).


Comparative diagnostic vs a sibling: logistic regression hands you coefficients — a single global, interpretable boundary you can write down and reason about (“the odds rise with X”). kNN hands you a local vote — no global rule, but a boundary that bends to the data wherever it needs to. This is the parametric-vs-non-parametric trade (Lecture 2, slide 9/10): the logistic model generalizes from a fixed form and few parameters; kNN’s complexity grows with the data and lives entirely in K and the metric. Match the choice to the question — interpretable global effect, or flexible local fit.

title: k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN)
text:
7. Past-exam lens

How kNN shows up. In the Spring-2025 take-home, Assignment 4 (“Predictive classification challenge” on SimulatedData.csv, exercises 4.1–4.9, phase0/exam_spring2025_notebook.md), kNN is named as a candidate classifier. Two exercises bear on it directly: 4.3 asks you to “encode categoricals, scale if necessary” and explicitly notes that “trees may not need scaling; distance/gradient models like k-NN or logistic regression do” — so if you submit kNN, the scaling decision from §3/§4 is being graded. 4.4 asks for at least two classifiers (a simple baseline plus a more complex model) with justification, 4.5 for hyperparameter tuning via CV (for kNN that is choosing K, §2/§4), and 4.6 for accuracy/precision/recall/F1. Crucially, 4.8 is run by the grader on a hidden hold-out test set, so your preprocessing (the scaler!) must be wired into a pipeline that generalizes to unseen rows — a raw, unscaled kNN that “worked” on your split will misfire on theirs. The data is simulated with “non-linear effects and noise,” which is the regime where a non-parametric method like kNN can shine — or, if you skip scaling and ignore the curse of dimensionality, quietly fail. kNN has not appeared as a stand-alone derivation question; it appears as a baseline classifier to deploy and justify.

title: k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN)
text:
8. Math


Math is off. Use the Math toggle in the top bar to show the course-level derivation (and “full” for the rigorous version).


Mode A — course level. (Throughout, K is the number of neighbors; the course/sklearn write this as k/n_neighbors, and p is the number of features — see the notation table.) kNN has nothing to fit; the whole method is a distance and a vote. The course defines distance as the Euclidean metric (notebook 03_Supervised_learning_with_kNN (1).ipynb, cell 3; Lecture 2, slide 8/10 names Euclidean as the metric “that matters”) — between a query x and a training point x' in p features, d(x,x') = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{p}\bigl(x_j - x'_j\bigr)^2}, which is exactly what the from-scratch code computes, np.sqrt(np.sum((x - y)**2)) (cell 7). Because every coordinate enters in its raw units, a feature on a larger numeric scale dominates the sum — the algebraic reason scaling is mandatory (§3, Example 3).
To predict, take the set \mathcal{N}_K(x) of the K training points with the smallest d(x,x') (the code’s np.argsort(distances)[:K]) and vote. For classification with classes c, assign the majority label, \hat{y}(x) = \arg\max_{c}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}_K(x)} \mathbb{1}[\,y_i = c\,], which the notebook implements as np.bincount(...).argmax() (cell 7). For regression the same neighborhood is averaged, \hat{y}(x) = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}_K(x)} y_i (Lecture 2, slide 8/10 — kNN does “classification (label) + regression (value)”). The sklearn default weights='uniform' gives every neighbor an equal vote; the weighted-vote variant weights='distance' weights neighbor i by 1/d(x,x_i), letting closer points count more (§3).
Reading K as the bias–variance dial. K=1 copies the nearest label, so the boundary chases individual points — high variance; large K averages over a wide neighborhood and washes out local structure toward the global majority — high bias (Lecture 2, slide 8/10). The course’s prescription is therefore to choose K by cross-validation, never off the test set (Lecture 2, slide 8/10; Example 2). The rigorous version of “why distances stop being informative as p grows,” and the asymptotic optimality that justifies kNN at all, are in Mode B. Foundations: linear-algebra essentials.


Mode B — full rigor. (Supplemental — the course slides treat kNN conceptually only, Lecture 2 slide 8/10. Anchored to ESL §13.3 “k-Nearest-Neighbor Classifiers” (printed pp. 463–468) and ESL §2.5 “Local Methods in High Dimensions” (printed pp. 22–25), with ISL §2.2.3 for the Bayes connection.)
The Bayes target. kNN is best understood as an estimator of the Bayes classifier, the rule that minimizes test error by assigning x_0 to the class j maximizing \Pr(Y=j \mid X=x_0) (ISL eq. 2.10). Its error, the irreducible Bayes error rate 1 - \mathrm{E}\!\bigl[\max_j \Pr(Y=j\mid X)\bigr] (ISL eq. 2.11), is the floor no classifier can beat. Since the conditional distribution is unknown, kNN estimates it by the neighborhood frequency, \Pr(Y=j \mid X=x_0) \approx \frac{1}{K}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}_0} \mathbb{1}(y_i = j) \qquad \text{(ISL eq. 2.12),} then classifies to the largest. ESL writes the same memory-based rule with Euclidean distance d_{(i)} = \lVert x_{(i)} - x_0 \rVert (ESL eq. 13.1), noting one “first standardize[s] each of the features to have mean zero and variance 1” (ESL §13.3) — the rigorous statement of §3’s scaling rule.
1-NN error ≤ 2× Bayes (Cover–Hart). ESL gives the classic asymptotic bound. Let k^\ast be the dominant class at x and p_k(x) the true conditional probability of class k. Then the Bayes error is 1 - p_{k^\ast}(x) (ESL eq. 13.2), while the asymptotic 1-nearest-neighbor error is the probability the query and its (asymptotically coincident) neighbor disagree: \text{1-NN error} = \sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k(x)\,\bigl(1 - p_k(x)\bigr) \;\ge\; 1 - p_{k^\ast}(x) \qquad \text{(ESL eqs. 13.3–13.4).} In the two-class case this is 2\,p_{k^\ast}(x)\bigl(1-p_{k^\ast}(x)\bigr) \le 2\bigl(1-p_{k^\ast}(x)\bigr) — at most twice the Bayes rate (Cover & Hart, 1967; ESL §13.3). The general-K refinement is \sum_k p_k(1-p_k) \le 2(1-p_{k^\ast}) - \tfrac{K}{K-1}(1-p_{k^\ast})^2 (ESL eq. 13.5). The catch is the “kicker” ESL flags: this assumes the bias is zero — true only asymptotically, when the data fill the space densely enough that the nearest neighbor coincides with the query. That assumption is exactly what the curse of dimensionality destroys.
Curse of dimensionality. In high p, neighbors are not near. ESL §2.5 makes this precise: to capture a fraction r of uniformly-distributed data with a hypercubical neighborhood, the expected edge length is e_p(r) = r^{1/p}, so in p=10 dimensions, capturing just 1% of the data needs e_{10}(0.01) = 0.63 and 10% needs e_{10}(0.1) = 0.80 of the entire range of every feature (ESL §2.5, Fig. 2.6) — the “neighborhood” is no longer local. Equivalently, the median distance from the origin to its nearest of N points is d(p,N) = \bigl(1 - \tfrac{1}{2}^{1/N}\bigr)^{1/p} (ESL eq. 2.24), which grows toward the boundary as p rises, and the sampling density scales as N^{1/p}, so matching a one-dimensional density of N_1=100 at p=10 would need 100^{10} points (ESL §2.5). ISL §3.5 confirms the practical consequence: as noise predictors are added (Fig. 3.20), KNN’s test MSE degrades far faster than a parametric model’s, because “spreading [the] observations over p … dimensions results in a phenomenon in which a given observation has no nearby neighbors” (ISL §3.5, curse of dimensionality). This is why §2/§6 push dimension reduction (PCA) or a feature-selecting model before kNN in wide data — and why K must be tuned by cross-validation (ESL Fig. 13.4 plots exactly this train/test/10-fold-CV-vs-K trade-off). See the linear-algebra appendix.

title: Logistic Regression
text: Linear family · the default first classifier for a binary target, and the linear-boundary baseline every other classifier is judged against. It is the classification analogue of OLS — same linear machinery, aimed at a probability instead of a continuous number. Siblings: LDA (also a linear boundary, but assumes Gaussian classes with shared covariance), Adaline (the same gradient-descent update, with MSE + linear activation instead of cross-entropy + sigmoid), kNN and Decision Trees (non-parametric, non-linear alternatives).

title: Logistic Regression
text:
1. Essence
Logistic regression predicts the probability that an observation belongs to the positive class. It does so with the same linear core as OLS — one coefficient per predictor plus an intercept, combined into a single number z = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p (the net input) — but then passes that number through the sigmoid function \sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z}), which squashes any real value into [0,1] so it can be read as a probability (Lecture 4, slide 7/11). To turn a probability into a class label you apply a threshold, by default 0.5: predict class 1 when \sigma(z) \ge 0.5, else class 0 (Lecture 8, slide 24/29). Despite the name, it is a classification technique, not a regression one (notebook 06_Logistic_regression.ipynb, cell 1).
The reason the linear-plus-sigmoid form is natural, not arbitrary, is that it makes the log-odds linear in the predictors: \log\!\big(\pi/(1-\pi)\big) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \dots + \beta_p x_p, where \pi is the probability of the positive class (Lecture 4, slide 6/11; the course slides and notebooks write this probability as p — here we use \pi to avoid colliding with p = number of predictors, see the notation table). This gives each coefficient a clean reading: a one-unit increase in z multiplies the odds \pi/(1-\pi) by e \approx 2.718 (Lecture 4, slide 8/11). That interpretability — coefficients as effects on the log-odds — is the whole appeal, the same way it is for OLS.
It is a parametric model fit by maximum likelihood (equivalently, by minimizing the negative log-likelihood, i.e. the cross-entropy loss). Compared with its nearest neighbors: LDA draws a linear boundary too but gets there by modelling each class as Gaussian with a shared covariance — logistic regression makes no distributional assumption about the predictors and estimates the boundary directly; Adaline is the identical gradient-descent learner with the sigmoid swapped for a linear activation and cross-entropy swapped for MSE (Lecture 8, slides 27–28/29); and kNN and trees drop the linear-boundary assumption entirely.

title: Logistic Regression
section: 2. When to use / when not to use
text:
2. When to use / when not to use

Reach for logistic regression when…

The target is a class (binary first; multi-class via One-vs-All or softmax) and you want calibrated probabilities, not just a hard label — e.g. “chance of survival”, “chance of disease” (Lecture 8, slide 24/29).
You want interpretable coefficients: each \beta_j is the change in log-odds per unit of x_j, and e^{\beta_j} is the odds multiplier — the classification counterpart of reading OLS slopes.
You expect a roughly linear decision boundary in the feature space (or one you can linearize with transforms/interactions).
You need a fast, transparent baseline before reaching for trees or neural nets. It is a natural candidate classifier for the Spring-2025 exam’s classification task (see §7).



Reach for something else when…

The classes are well-separated Gaussians with similar covariance → LDA uses that structure and can be more stable, especially with little data or perfectly separable classes (where plain logistic regression’s coefficients can diverge). Lecture 4 (slide 4/11) lists LDA’s assumptions explicitly.
The boundary is clearly non-linear and you don’t want to hand-engineer the form → Decision Trees / Random Forests (axis-aligned splits) or kNN capture curvature automatically.
You want raw flexibility / a stepping stone to neural nets → a single sigmoid unit is logistic regression; stacking them gives an MLP. Adaline is the same learner with a linear output.
Predictors heavily outnumber observations or are strongly correlated → coefficients become unstable; use the built-in L2/L1 penalty (the C/penalty arguments, §3) — the classification echo of Ridge/Lasso.

title: Logistic Regression
text:
3. Code idiom
The canonical course idiom is scikit-learn’s LogisticRegression (notebook 06, on Titanic); the course also builds the model from scratch by gradient descent (notebook 15, on Iris) to show the sigmoid + cross-entropy mechanics — and to make the Adaline → logistic link concrete.
Canonical (sklearn) — (notebook 06_Logistic_regression.ipynb, cell 7)
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

log_reg = LogisticRegression(solver='lbfgs', max_iter=500)  # lbfgs = quasi-Newton optimizer
log_reg.fit(X_train, y_train)                                # X: (n_samples, n_features), y in {0,1}
log_reg.predict(X_test)                                      # hard labels at the 0.5 threshold
log_reg.predict_proba(X_test)                                # [P(class 0), P(class 1)] per row
log_reg.coef_        # the log-odds slopes β₁…β_p
log_reg.intercept_   # the intercept β₀
solver='lbfgs' is the optimizer (a quasi-Newton method); max_iter=500 raises the iteration cap from the default 100 so the optimizer converges on this data. Everything else is default: penalty='l2', C=1.0 (inverse regularization strength — smaller C means stronger shrinkage, the classification analogue of a larger Ridge alpha), class_weight=None. For imbalanced classes, class_weight='balanced' and tuning C/penalty are the standard knobs (real sklearn parameters; values left default as they are not changed in the notebook).
From scratch — gradient descent (notebook 15_LogisticRegression.ipynb, cell id a342d4e2). This is Adaline with two changes: a sigmoid activation and a cross-entropy loss. Per Lecture 8 (slides 27–28/29) the gradient-descent update is unchanged — both reduce to -\tfrac1n\sum(y-\text{activation})\,x_j — only the activation inside differs ([disagreements R9-11]):
class LogisticRegressionGD:
    def __init__(self, eta=0.01, n_iter=50, random_state=1):   # course uses eta=0.3, n_iter=1000
        self.eta = eta; self.n_iter = n_iter; self.random_state = random_state

    def fit(self, X, y):
        rgen = np.random.RandomState(self.random_state)
        self.w_ = rgen.normal(loc=0.0, scale=0.01, size=X.shape[1])  # small random init
        self.b_ = 0.0
        self.losses_ = []
        for i in range(self.n_iter):
            output = self.activation(self.net_input(X))      # σ(z), the predicted probability
            errors = (y - output)                            # y − σ(z)
            self.w_ += self.eta * X.T.dot(errors) / X.shape[0]   # vectorized GD step (÷ n)
            self.b_ += self.eta * errors.mean()
            output_clipped = np.clip(output, 1e-10, 1.0 - 1e-10)         # avoid log(0)
            loss = -y.dot(np.log(output_clipped)) - (1 - y).dot(np.log(1 - output_clipped))
            self.losses_.append(loss / X.shape[0])           # binary cross-entropy per sample

    def net_input(self, X):   return np.dot(X, self.w_) + self.b_       # z = w·x + b
    def activation(self, z):  return 1. / (1. + np.exp(-np.clip(z, -250, 250)))  # sigmoid (clipped)
    def predict(self, X):     return np.where(self.activation(self.net_input(X)) >= 0.5, 1, 0)
The course instantiates this with LogisticRegressionGD(eta=0.3, n_iter=1000, random_state=1) (cell id 50ee34c8) — a learning rate eta (\eta) of 0.3 and n_iter 1000 epochs, well above the class defaults eta=0.01, n_iter=50.

Idiom variation worth knowing — multi-class via One-vs-All. For 3 classes the from-scratch notebook trains one binary detector per class and stacks their sigmoid outputs, then takes the argmax (notebook 15_LogisticRegression.ipynb, cell id f4432549):
probabilities = np.zeros((X.shape[0], 3))
for k in range(3):
    y_k = np.where(y_all == k, 1, 0)                 # class k vs the rest
    lrgd_k = LogisticRegressionGD(eta=0.3, n_iter=1000, random_state=1).fit(X, y_k)
    probabilities[:, k] = lrgd_k.activation(lrgd_k.net_input(X))
predicted = np.argmax(probabilities, axis=1)         # pick the most confident detector
The notebook explicitly warns these three sigmoid outputs do not sum to 1 — each is an independent binary detector; for true probabilities that sum to 1 you would use softmax (multinomial) regression instead (cell id 6b3b3496). sklearn’s LogisticRegression does softmax/OvA automatically when y has more than two classes.

title: Logistic Regression
text:
4. Worked examples

Example 1 — Titanic survival with sklearn
The course’s canonical example predicts survival on the Titanic training set (notebook 06_Logistic_regression.ipynb, cells 3–11). After dropna() the 891-row frame collapses to 183 rows (the sparse Cabin column drives most of the loss, biasing the sample toward 1st-class passengers — a real data quirk the notebook does not flag), Sex is encoded male=1/female=0, and six features are used with an 80/20 split (random_state=15):
df = pd.read_csv('../data/titanic/train.csv').dropna()        # 891 → 183 rows
df['Sex'] = df['Sex'].apply(lambda x: 1 if x == 'male' else 0)
X = df[['Pclass', 'Sex', 'Age', 'SibSp', 'Parch', 'Fare']]
y = df['Survived']
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=15)
log_reg = LogisticRegression(solver='lbfgs', max_iter=500).fit(X_train, y_train)
This yields test accuracy ≈ 0.892 (33/37 correct), well above either trivial baseline (the 37-row test set is 20 survived / 17 died, so always-guessing the majority class “survived” scores 0.541 and always-guessing “died” scores 0.459) — (computed via the course venv, random_state=15; the notebook stores no outputs). The confusion matrix is [[13, 4], [0, 20]]: every actual survivor is caught (recall 1.00 for class 1) at the cost of 4 false alarms (class-0 recall 0.76). The fitted coefficients read directly as log-odds effects:
