How to use this with the rest of the site

Stuck on an exercise? Find its row above and open the listed prerequisite method pages first — those are the exact methods its solution uses.
Revising a method? Trace its node in the map back to the exercises that exercise it — that gives you ready-made practice problems for that method.
Cross-method practice: exercises 03–05 are where methods compete on one dataset. For head-to-head comparisons on shared datasets see the Showdowns page; for choosing among them see the Decision Dashboard and Family Comparisons.

title: Showdowns

The classification showdown lines up Logistic Regression, LDA, kNN, a Decision Tree and a Random Forest on a shared 2-D boundary; the regression showdown lines up OLS, Ridge, Lasso, a Tree and a Random Forest on Hitters. Figure 2: Regression showdown on Hitters (263 rows, 16 features, 75/25 split, random_state=1, computed via the course .venv): test R² (left, higher is better) and test RMSE in $1000s (right, lower is better) for five regressors. Linear models in blue (OLS, Ridge, Lasso), tree models in green (Tree, RF). What to notice: plain OLS is the weakest (test R²≈0.36) — it overfits the 16 partly-redundant career-total predictors; Ridge and Lasso shrink those coefficients and edge test R² up to ≈0.38–0.39; the depth-3 single Tree (0.37) is no better than OLS; but the depth-3 Random Forest jumps to test R²≈0.59 / RMSE≈$304k, comfortably the best — averaging 100 shallow trees captures the non-linear structure the linear models miss while controlling the variance a single tree cannot.




Reading it — OLS overfits, shrinkage helps a little, the forest helps a lot. Plain OLS is the weakest of the five: test R^2 = 0.36 against a train R^2 = 0.55, the wide train–test gap that is the fingerprint of variance (OLS §4, §6). The cause is structural — 16 partly-redundant career totals (CAtBat, CHits, CRuns… all move together), so OLS fits the training sample’s noise. This is precisely the diagnosis the OLS page makes and the cue it hands to regularization.
Ridge and Lasso, with cross-validated alpha, do exactly what regularization §4 predicts: they trade a little training fit (train R^2 0.55 → 0.54) for better generalization (test R^2 0.36 → 0.38–0.39, RMSE 377 → 370–373). The gain is modest but real — the bias–variance trade-off made concrete, and the reasoning the exam grades. Note that a penalty cannot fix a wrong functional form: if the Salary surface is genuinely non-linear, shrinking linear coefficients only goes so far (regularization §2: “a penalty cannot fix a wrong functional form”).
The two tree-family models bracket the lesson. A single depth-3 Tree reaches test R^2 = 0.37 — no better than OLS — while its train R^2 (0.74) already shows the high-variance, memorize-the-sample behaviour decision-trees §1/§5 describes; “a single tree’s variance can’t be cross-validated away, only ensembled away.” And that is exactly what the depth-3 Random Forest does: averaging 100 decorrelated shallow trees lifts test R^2 to 0.59 and cuts RMSE to $304k — comfortably the best model here. It captures the non-linear, interaction-heavy structure the linear models cannot, while the bagging-plus-feature-randomness of random-forests §1 controls the variance a lone tree cannot. The ordering — RF ≫ Ridge ≈ Lasso > Tree ≈ OLS — is the cross-method story in one line: when the truth is non-linear with redundant predictors, an ensemble of shallow trees beats both the linear baseline and its regularized fixes.

How a showdown maps to the exam. The Spring-2025 take-home runs these comparisons separately — Assignment 1 is OLS-vs-Ridge-vs-Lasso on Hitters (the left three bars), Assignment 3 is Tree-vs-Random-Forest-vs-boosting on WDBC. This page puts the regression contenders on one axis to make the relative gains legible: the marks reward (i) diagnosing OLS’s variance from the train–test gap, (ii) justifying why shrinkage narrows it, and (iii) explaining why a non-linear ensemble can leap past all the linear models when the relationship isn’t linear. See the decision dashboard for the “which model when” summary and each method page’s §7 for the per-assignment detail.

title: Showdowns
text:
3. What the two showdowns share
Both panels are the same idea told twice. In classification, model choice changes the shape of the boundary — linear (Logistic/LDA), local-wiggly (kNN), or axis-aligned-blocky (Tree/RF) — and the right choice depends on the true boundary’s geometry. In regression, model choice changes how the bias–variance budget is spent — OLS pays in variance, Ridge/Lasso buy it back with a little bias, a single Tree overfits, and the Forest spends its budget on decorrelated averaging to win. The unifying lens is bias–variance, and the practical “pick one” guide is the decision dashboard; every method’s own §2 (“when to use / when not”) is the per-model version of the same advice.

title: Drill: Titanic Preprocessing
text: Foundations / preprocessing drill · The one exercise that is pure data preparation — no model is fitted. Load the raw Titanic table, fix missing values, tame outliers, encode the categoricals, and read survival straight off the data as conditional probabilities.

title: Drill: Titanic Preprocessing
text:
1. What this exercise teaches
Hands-on preprocessing and EDA on a real, messy tabular dataset: load and inspect, impute missing values, treat outliers (focus on Fare), encode Sex and Embarked, and compute survival probabilities by group. It is the drill that builds the habits every later modelling exercise assumes — the data-cleaning that happens before any estimator.

This is the only no-model exercise. Every other drill starts from cleaned data or a sklearn toy dataset. Here the whole task is the cleaning. Treat it as the canonical worked example of Pattern F — Missing data handling and the diagnostics in Reading the Data.

title: Drill: Titanic Preprocessing
text:
2. Setup

Dataset: the Kaggle Titanic training set, train.csv (891 passengers). Locally it lives at course_materials/Data/Titanic data/train.csv (note the space in the folder name), so a loader call is pd.read_csv("course_materials/Data/Titanic data/train.csv"). The stub itself names only the bare filename train.csv and gives no loader.
Columns referenced by the prompt: Fare, Sex, Embarked, Survived (the 0/1 target), and passenger class. The actual CSV header is PassengerId, Survived, Pclass, Name, Sex, Age, SibSp, Parch, Ticket, Fare, Cabin, Embarked (verified against the local file).
Target (implied): Survived (0/1) — the survival-probability questions are means of this column.
Task: preprocessing + descriptive analysis. No train/test split, no estimator, no fit.
Expected output: a cleaned DataFrame, a stated imputation/outlier strategy, encoded categoricals, and computed survival probabilities by class and by sex, plus a short written discussion of what passenger class represents and why preprocessing matters.


The stub writes pclass (lowercase); the real column is Pclass. The Kaggle CSV capitalizes Pclass, Survived, Sex, Embarked, and Fare. Code that hard-codes the lowercase pclass from the prompt raises KeyError. Always check the header with df.columns before indexing. (Verified against the local train.csv header.)

title: Drill: Titanic Preprocessing
text:
3. Walkthrough
There is no _VHL solution notebook for this topic — the stub is a single markdown cell with a seven-part prompt and no code. The walkthrough below is therefore a sketch of the standard decisions the prompt asks for, anchored to the Reading the Data diagnostics rather than to stored solution cells. No numbers or outputs are reproduced because none exist to cite.
Decision 1 — load and inspect (prompt part 1). df.head(), df.info(), df.describe(). The point of info() here is to surface the missingness: it prints non-null counts per column, which is how you discover that Age, Cabin, and Embarked are incomplete — see Diagnostic 2 — Missingness.
Decision 2 — impute missing values (prompt part 2). Three columns, three different calls:

Age (~177 missing) — fill with the median, not the mean, because the age distribution is right-skewed and the median is robust to that skew: df["Age"].fillna(df["Age"].median()).
Embarked (a couple missing) — fill with the mode (most common port): df["Embarked"].fillna(df["Embarked"].mode()[0]).
Cabin (~77% missing) — too sparse to impute; the usual move is to drop the column rather than invent values.

The key idiom is choosing the statistic to match the column’s type and shape (median for skewed numeric, mode for categorical) — not a single blanket rule.
Decision 3 — outliers on Fare (prompt part 3). Fare is heavily right-skewed (a handful of very high first-class fares). Inspect with df["Fare"].describe() or a boxplot, then decide: cap at a high quantile (winsorize) or leave them, but do not blindly delete — the extreme fares are legitimate first-class tickets that carry real survival signal. The decision and its justification are what the prompt grades.
Decision 4 — encode categoricals (prompt part 4). Sex is binary → label-encode to 0/1 (df["Sex"].map({"male": 0, "female": 1})). Embarked is nominal with three levels → one-hot encode (pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["Embarked"])), which produces the C/Q/S indicator columns. The idiom worth internalizing: binary → label, multi-level nominal → one-hot.
Decision 5 — survival probabilities (prompt parts 5–6). Because Survived is 0/1, a survival probability is just its group mean:
df.groupby("Pclass")["Survived"].mean()    # survival rate by class
df.groupby("Sex")["Survived"].mean()        # survival rate male vs female
This is the conceptual heart of the exercise: a conditional probability P(Survived | group) read directly off the data as a groupby(...).mean(). The written parts (6–7) then ask what Pclass represents (a socio-economic proxy: 1st/2nd/3rd) and why this cleaning matters before any model.

title: Drill: Titanic Preprocessing
text:
4. Common pitfalls


Mean vs median for Age. Using the mean on a skewed column pulls imputed values toward the long tail; median is the safer default. (See Diagnostic 2.)
Deleting Fare outliers wholesale discards real first-class passengers and biases survival rates downward for that group.
Lowercase pclass — the prompt’s spelling does not match the CSV’s Pclass; will KeyError.
Forgetting that Survived is binary — “survival probability” is mean() of the 0/1 column; computing a count or a sum instead answers a different question.
One-hot vs label for Embarked — label-encoding a 3-level nominal (S=0, C=1, Q=2) invents a false ordering; use one-hot. Sex is the exception because it is binary.
Imputing Cabin — at ~77% missing there is nothing reliable to impute; drop it.

title: Drill: Titanic Preprocessing
section: 5. What this exercise teaches that the others don’t
text:
5. What this exercise teaches that the others don’t
It is the only drill focused purely on raw-data preprocessing and EDA — missing-value imputation, outlier treatment, and categorical encoding — with no estimator at all. It is also the only one that asks you to compute conditional probabilities directly from a real tabular dataset as descriptive statistics (groupby().mean() on a 0/1 target), rather than getting them out of a fitted classifier. Every modelling drill silently assumes these steps are already done; this one makes them the whole job.

text:

title: Drill: Predicting House Prices
text: Regression drill — Linear family · End-to-end regression on the Ames house-prices data: numeric-only cleaning, standardize both X and y, fit OLS → Ridge → Lasso, compare in- vs out-of-sample MSE/R², select features with Lasso, and close with an inverse-transform “what-if” price predictor.

title: Drill: Predicting House Prices
text:
1. What this exercise teaches
The full regularized-regression workflow on real, messy data: clean to numeric and drop missing rows, standardize, fit OLS as a baseline, then Ridge and Lasso, reading the in-sample-vs-out-of-sample gap as the bias–variance story, then use Lasso for feature selection and inverse-transform predictions back to dollars.

This is the worked instance of Workflow Pattern B — regression with many predictors. It is also the exercise companion to the exam’s Assignment 1 (OLS vs Ridge vs Lasso on Hitters.csv): same reasoning, different dataset. The graded skill is the justification — why shrinkage narrows the train–test gap — at least as much as the code.

title: Drill: Predicting House Prices
text:
2. Setup

Dataset: Kaggle “House Prices — Advanced Regression Techniques” (Ames, Iowa). 1,460 rows, 81 columns. Locally at course_materials/Data/house-prices data/train.csv (note the space in the folder name; the notebook’s own path is ../../data/house-prices/train.csv).
Loader (solution cell-2): data = pd.read_csv('../../data/house-prices/train.csv').
Target: SalePrice.
Feature set after cleaning: the 37 numeric columns (the categorical columns are dropped entirely).
Task: continuous-target regression; report in-sample and out-of-sample MSE and R² for OLS, Ridge, and Lasso.
Expected output: MSE/R² for all three models (in- and out-of-sample); the 10 most important Lasso features; MSE/R² for OLS re-fit on just those 10; and a function that returns un-normalized predicted prices for edited feature vectors.

title: Drill: Predicting House Prices
text:
3. Walkthrough
Idioms and stored numeric outputs are transcribed from 03_Predicting_house_prices_VHL.ipynb (cells cited). All metrics below are the exact saved cell outputs, and are on the standardized y scale.
Decision 1 — split before cleaning (cell-3). X = data.drop("SalePrice", axis=1), y = data["SalePrice"], then train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.33, random_state=10). Note random_state=10 (not the usual 42) — selected features and metrics are split-dependent.
Decision 2 — numeric-only, drop NaN rows, re-align y (cell-4).
numeric_cols = X_train.select_dtypes(include=['int64', 'float64']).columns
X_train_num  = X_train[numeric_cols].dropna()       # drops any row with a numeric NaN
y_train_num  = y_train.loc[X_train_num.index]       # KEY: re-align y to surviving rows
The load-bearing idiom is y_train.loc[X_train_num.index]: dropna() removes rows, so y must be re-indexed to match or X and y silently desync. Categorical columns are dropped wholesale — simpler, but it discards signal (ordinal integers like OverallQual survive because they’re stored as ints).
Decision 3 — standardize X and y with separate scalers (cell-5).
scaler_x = StandardScaler().fit(X_train_num)
scaler_y = StandardScaler().fit(y_train_num.values.reshape(-1, 1))
# transform train and test; keep DataFrames so index/columns survive
Two scalers because y is scaled too — this is why the reported MSE/R² are on the standardized scale, and why the prediction function later needs scaler_y.inverse_transform. Both scalers are fit on train only.
Decision 4 — OLS baseline (cells 6–8). LinearRegression() on the standardized data. Stored outputs:



OLS

Decision 5 — Ridge and Lasso (cells 9–11). Ridge(alpha=0.5) and Lasso(alpha=0.01), same fit/predict API. Stored outputs:

Lasso is best out-of-sample (lowest test MSE 0.1729, highest test R² 0.8254) despite the worst in-sample fit — the textbook signature of regularization trading a little training fit for better generalization.
Decision 6 — Lasso feature selection (cell-12). Re-fit Lasso(alpha=0.01), then wrap it:
sfm = SelectFromModel(lasso, max_features=10)
sfm.fit(X_train_norm, y_train_norm)
important_features = X_train_norm.columns[sfm.get_support()]
The 10 selected features (stored output): MSSubClass, LotArea, OverallQual, OverallCond, YearBuilt, MasVnrArea, BsmtFinSF1, GrLivArea, BsmtFullBath, GarageCars.
Decision 7 — re-fit OLS on the 10 features (cell-13). LinearRegression() on X_train_norm[important_features]. Stored output: MSE 0.1784, R² 0.8198 — almost identical to the full 37-feature OLS (0.1760 / 0.8223) using only 10 features, which is the whole point of selection.
Decision 8 — inverse-transform “what-if” predictor (cell-14).
def inspectPrediction(model, observed_units):
    pred = model.predict(pd.DataFrame(scaler_x.transform(observed_units),
                                      index=observed_units.index,
                                      columns=observed_units.columns))
    return scaler_y.inverse_transform(pred.reshape(-1, 1))   # back to dollars
It scales the inputs in, predicts on the standardized scale, then scaler_y.inverse_transform brings the prediction back to dollar prices — letting you edit a feature (e.g. raise OverallQual) and see the price change.
Hyperparameters (exact): train_test_split(test_size=0.33, random_state=10); LinearRegression() defaults; Ridge(alpha=0.5); Lasso(alpha=0.01) (used for both fitting and selection); SelectFromModel(max_features=10) (default threshold); StandardScaler() defaults.

title: Drill: Predicting House Prices
text:
4. Common pitfalls


dropna() desyncs X and y unless you re-align with y_train.loc[X_train_num.index]. Columns like LotFrontage, MasVnrArea, GarageYrBlt carry NaNs that drop rows.
Metrics are on the standardized y scale, not dollars. An MSE of 0.17 is meaningless until you remember y was standardized — and the predictor must inverse_transform y to report dollars.
random_state=10, not 42. Selected features and every metric are split-dependent; a different seed gives a different “10 most important”.
Lasso(alpha=0.01) is deliberately small. Too large an alpha zeros most coefficients, and then SelectFromModel(max_features=10) can return fewer than 10 surviving features.
SelectFromModel(max_features=10) still applies a default importance threshold — max_features is a cap, not a guarantee; results shift with alpha.
Dropping all categoricals loses signal. The model is numeric-only for simplicity; in practice you’d encode the informative categoricals.
alpha is λ, not the Elastic-Net mix. In scikit-learn the alpha argument is the penalty strength λ; the mixing ratio is the separate l1_ratio. See the regularization page pitfall.

title: Drill: Model Selection & Evaluation
text: Cross-cutting drill · The methodology exercise: pick kNN’s k by cross-validation, compare classifiers via accuracy and confusion matrices, run 5-fold CV across a model zoo, and tune a Decision Tree with GridSearchCV — all on Iris, where the point is the evaluation machinery, not winning accuracy.

title: Drill: Model Selection & Evaluation
text:
What this exercise teaches
The model-selection and evaluation workflow rather than building any single model: using cross_val_score to choose a hyperparameter, reading ConfusionMatrixDisplay, comparing models with k-fold CV, and running a systematic GridSearchCV. It is the only exercise centred on the evaluation tools themselves.

title: Drill: Model Selection & Evaluation
text:
Setup

Dataset: Iris, built into sklearn — from sklearn.datasets import load_iris; iris = load_iris(); X, y = iris.data, iris.target. 150 samples, 4 features, 3 species classes. iris.target_names (setosa / versicolor / virginica) are used as confusion-matrix labels. No external file.
Target: iris.target — three classes.
Task: four code parts (kNN+CV, accuracy+confusion matrix, multi-model k-fold CV, GridSearchCV on a tree) plus a fifth, discussion-only part on ROC / Precision-Recall.
Expected output: a CV-accuracy-vs-k curve; per-model accuracy and confusion-matrix heatmaps; a 5-fold-CV accuracy bar chart across models; the tree’s best hyperparameters, best CV score, and feature importances. Note: this VHL export has no saved cell outputs — the code is verified but the exact accuracy numbers were not stored, so none are quoted below.

title: Drill: Model Selection & Evaluation
text:
Walkthrough
Part 1 — choose k by cross-validation (VHL cell 2). The defining idiom: loop over candidate k, take the mean of a 5-fold cross_val_score, and plot accuracy vs k. CV (not a single train/test split) is what makes the choice stable on a 150-row dataset:
k_values = range(1, 15)          # note: stops at 14 — range is exclusive
cv_scores = []
for k in k_values:
    knn = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)
    scores = cross_val_score(knn, X, y, cv=5)
    cv_scores.append(scores.mean())
The curve is the deliverable: small k overfits (high variance), large k over-smooths (high bias) — read the best k off the peak. See kNN.
Part 2 — accuracy + confusion matrix (VHL cell 3). Three models in a dict, each fit / predicted / scored, with a confusion-matrix heatmap per model:
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.8, random_state=42)  # 80% TEST
models = {
    'kNN (k=5))': KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5),
    'Decision Tree': DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42),
    'Logistic Regression': LogisticRegression(max_iter=200, random_state=42),
}
for name, model in models.items():
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
    acc = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)
    ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred),
                           display_labels=iris.target_names).plot(cmap=plt.cm.Blues)
The confusion matrix is the point: on Iris, errors concentrate at the versicolor / virginica boundary (the two overlapping species), which a single accuracy number hides.
Part 3 — k-fold CV across a model zoo (VHL cell 4). Four models, each scored with cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5).mean(), then bar-charted. Note kNN here uses n_neighbors=10 (vs k=5 in Part 2) and SVM is SVC(probability=True, random_state=42):
models_cv = {
    'kNN': KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=10),
    'Decision Tree': DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42),
    'Logistic Regression': LogisticRegression(max_iter=200, random_state=42),
    'SVM': SVC(probability=True, random_state=42),
}
Part 4 — systematic tuning with GridSearchCV (VHL cell 5). The contrast with Exercise 04’s manual loops: a grid, 5-fold CV, automatic best-estimator selection:
param_grid = {'max_depth': [None, 2, 3, 4, 5],
              'min_samples_leaf': [1, 2, 3],
              'min_samples_split': [2, 3, 4]}
grid_search = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42),
                           param_grid, cv=5, scoring='accuracy')
grid_search.fit(X, y)
grid_search.best_params_; grid_search.best_score_
grid_search.best_estimator_.feature_importances_
The decision worth noting: grid_search.fit(X, y) is run on the full dataset, so best_score_ is the cross-validated estimate, not held-out test accuracy — a legitimate answer to “evaluate via a test set or via CV,” choosing CV.
Part 5 — ROC & Precision-Recall is discussion-only. The source has no code here: it asks you to review the sklearn docs and answer conceptual questions (how ROC/PR generalize to multiclass, the threshold trade-off, when PR beats ROC, how to read AUC). Treat it as written discussion, not implementation.

Quirks baked into the source — know them.

test_size=0.8 (Part 2) trains on only 30 of 150 samples. That tiny training set inflates the variance of the accuracy/confusion-matrix comparison — easy to over-read. CV (Parts 1, 3, 4) is the more trustworthy basis here.
range(1, 15) stops at k=14, despite the prompt saying “1 to 15” (range is exclusive). Use range(1, 16) if you want 15 included.
GridSearchCV on full X, y gives a CV score, not a test score — don’t report best_score_ as held-out accuracy.
SVC(probability=True) runs an internal cross-validation to calibrate probabilities, slowing the fit; only set it if you actually need predict_proba (e.g. for ROC).
Cosmetic: the dict key 'kNN (k=5))' has an extra closing paren; harmless.

title: Drill: Model Selection & Evaluation
text:
Common pitfalls
Iris is small and easy, so accuracies sit near the ceiling and model differences are subtle — the lesson is the evaluation procedure, not which model wins. Quoting a single accuracy hides where the errors live (the confusion matrix shows it). And mixing up the two roles of CV here trips people up: in Part 1 CV selects a hyperparameter, in Part 4 it both selects and reports the score — keep selection and final evaluation conceptually separate when the stakes are real.

title: Drill: Model Selection & Evaluation
section: What this exercise teaches that the others don’t
text:
What this exercise teaches that the others don’t
It is the only exercise built around evaluation methodology instead of a single model: cross_val_score to pick k, ConfusionMatrixDisplay to see where errors fall, k-fold CV to compare models fairly, and GridSearchCV for systematic search. It is the only place tying k and tree depth to bias–variance through CV curves, and the only systematic (grid) hyperparameter search in the course. Exercise 04 does the manual version of the same idea; this drill is the disciplined upgrade.

Model selection is a loop, not a single fit: propose candidates → score each by cross-validation → inspect where the winner fails (confusion matrix) → tune systematically (grid search) → reserve a clean estimate for the final number. On a dataset this easy the accuracies barely move; the graded skill is running the loop and justifying each choice.

title: Notation
section: The five disambiguations to watch site-wide
text:
The five disambiguations to watch site-wide

k / K — the worst offender. Resolved by role-specific letters: K neighbors, d parameters, V folds, K clusters, K hidden units. Every math header names its local k.
p = probability vs #predictors — this site uses \pi for probability (slides write p).
sklearn alpha = \lambda (penalty strength), not the Elastic-Net \alpha (that is l1_ratio). The single most common regularization bug — flagged on the Regularization page.
\eta vs \alpha for learning rate — standardized on \eta.
\delta: update step vs error signal — standardized on ESL’s error signal \delta; the update step is \Delta\theta.
